articles.title: 'Deeply personal moment': Watch Sagal Abdi-Wali's by-election victory speech
articles.summary: Labour beat the Green Party with 45% of the vote in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election.
articles.body:
Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali has won the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, securing 45% of the vote and beating the Green Party which came in second place.

In her victory speech, the Camden Council leader reflected on how the borough had given her family a home and shaped her life.

"My commitment to this community runs deep," she said, adding that she hoped people who looked like her would see themselves reflected in Parliament.

articles.title: LIV Golf League timeline: Key moments from breakaway circuit's history, rivalry with the PGA Tour and what happens next
articles.summary: How has the LIV Golf League grown since its launch and what happens next for the circuit? Timeline of its breakthrough into the men's professional game and the challenges it faced over world rankings, funding changes and rivalries with other tours
articles.body:
Its arrival earlier in the decade sparked division and debate in a fractured men's game, with players leaving the PGA Tour and DP World Tour to join the breakaway circuit.

A shock framework agreement between the PGA Tour, DP World Tour and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) was unable to unify men's golf, with LIV Golf facing fresh challenges to retain its place in the sport.

From its initial inception and increasing growth through to players leaving and cuts in funding, we look at the timeline of LIV Golf's history so far...

October 2021: LIV Golf Investments was officially announced and two-time Open champion Greg Norman revealed as the league's founding CEO.

February 2022: In an interview with Golf Digest , Phil Mickelson criticised the PGA Tour's policy on player media rights. He said: "It was the tour's obnoxious greed that has really opened the door for opportunities elsewhere." He later told journalist Alan Shipnuck that the Saudis were "scary m************ to be involved with".

March 2022: LIV Golf announced it would launch an eight-tournament schedule on June 9 , titled the LIV Invitational Series. The total prize pot for the eight events was set at £191.32m ($255m).

May 2022: Norman branded the PGA Tour "anti-competitive" , after the US circuit denied players their release requests to play in LIV Golf events. Former Masters champions Dustin Johnson and Sergio Garcia were revealed among the first group of players to tee up at LIV's inaugural event in London.

June 2022: Mickelson confirmed he would play in LIV Golf's first event, won by Charl Schwartzel. The PGA Tour sent a letter to its members announcing those in the field at LIV Golf London were suspended indefinitely. Bryson DeChambeau and Brooks Koepka both joined the breakaway league ahead of its second event.

July 2022: The DP World Tour issued fines of £100,000 ($133,921) to LIV players who featured in LIV Golf London. Meanwhile, LIV Golf submitted an application for its players to be given Official World Golf Ranking (OWGR) points.

July 2022: Henrik Stenson sent shockwaves through the golfing world by joining LIV Golf and was subsequently stripped of his role as Team Europe's captain for the 2023 Ryder Cup in Italy .

August 2022: A group of 11 LIV Golf players, including Mickelson, Ian Poulter and Johnson, filed an antitrust lawsuit against the PGA Tour. LIV Golf later joined the lawsuit. After winning The Open at St Andrews and at the end of the PGA Tour season, Cameron Smith became the latest player to join LIV Golf .

September 2022: Rory McIlroy likened LIV Golf to a "soap opera" and said his relationship with some of his Ryder Cup team-mates who joined LIV had been damaged.

October 2022: The PGA Tour filed a federal lawsuit against Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) and Yasir Al-Rumayyan, the governor of the PIF.

November 2022: McIlroy called for Norman to leave the rebel league and Tiger Woods also encouraged Norman to go in order for a peace settlement to be negotiated.

December 2022: Augusta National chairman Fred Ridley confirmed eligible LIV Golfers could play at The Masters . Jon Rahm said PGA Tour players should be 'thankful' for LIV .

January 2023: Patrick Reed and McIlroy were involved in the 'tee-gate' saga, where Reed flicked a 4Aces GC tee at the Northern Irishman after the American accused McIlroy of ignoring him .

February 2023: The DP World Tour and LIV Golf went to court for an arbitration hearing, held over five days .

April 2023: The DP World Tour won its legal battle against players who elected to join LIV Golf , enabling them to impose £100,000 ($134,706) fines against LIV players for competing in conflicting events.

May 2023: Koepka became the first LIV Golfer to win a major at the PGA Championship, lifting the Wanamaker Trophy for a third time.

June 2023: The PGA Tour, DP World Tour and PIF announce a shock 'framework agreement' , where the organisations ended all pending lawsuits and said they wanted to cooperate to "unify the game of golf".

McIlroy hit back at the announcement, saying he felt like a "sacrificial lamb" , while PGA Tour commissioner Jay Monahan faced calls to resign .

October 2023: LIV Golf lost its initial bid to be awarded OWGR points .

December 2023: Rahm, who won The Masters in April, joined LIV Golf for a deal reportedly worth up to £450m ($607.7m).

January 2024: Tyrrell Hatton follows Rahm to LIV Golf for a then-reported fee of £47.3m ($60m).

February 2024: Anthony Kim ended a 12-year absence from professional golf by joining the breakaway league. McIlroy softened his stance on LIV Golf , saying players who joined the rebel league should be allowed to come back to the PGA Tour.

March 2024: Norman confirmed LIV Golf had withdrawn its application for OWGR points . Woods formed part of a delegation of PGA Tour members to meet with LIV Golf powerbrokers , including Al-Rumayyan, in the Bahamas, to discuss the merger. PGA Tour commissioner Monahan said the talks were "constructive".

April 2024: McIlroy denied claims he was previously close to joining LIV Golf.

June 2024: DeChambeau claimed a one-shot victory at the US Open , following Koepka as the second LIV player to win a major, after McIlroy's dramatic late collapse at Pinehurst No 2.

September 2024: The PGA of America confirmed LIV Golfers would be eligible to play for Team USA at the Ryder Cup the following year .

October 2024: Monahan and Al-Rumayyan played together at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship , signalling that merger talks were progressing.

January 2025: Norman was replaced as LIV Golf's CEO by Scot O'Neil . McIlroy praised Norman for "getting LIV Golf off the ground".

February 2025: Woods joined Al-Rumayyan and Adam Scott for talks at the White House with US President Donald Trump regarding the ongoing merger .

March 2025: Monahan said Trump's involvement in ongoing talks between golf's key stakeholders made the prospect of a reunification between the tours "very real".

November 2025: Having launched a fresh bid for OWGR points in July, LIV looked to enhance its push by expanding from 54-hole events to a 72-hole format, a move which McIlroy called "peculiar" .

December 2025: Koepka announced he was leaving LIV Golf due to personal reasons. He then confirmed his return to the PGA Tour via the Returning Member Program , where he was subjected to certain conditions and required to make a £3.7m ($5m) donation to charity.

January 2026: Reed also confirmed his departure from LIV Golf and returned to play on the DP World Tour .

February 2026: LIV Golf was granted world ranking points by the OWGR , but the breakaway league's bosses criticised the allocation of ranking points LIV players could receive - only the top 10 and ties - as "unfair".

The DP World Tour offered conditional releases to eight members, including Hatton , provided they paid off their outstanding fines. Rahm insisted he had "no intention" of paying his fines.

March 2026: Rahm withdrew his appeal against sanctions imposed by the DP World Tour for playing in conflicting LIV Golf events. His fines were believed to be around £2.2m ($3m). He said the tour's conditional release programme was "extorting players".

April 2026: The PIF confirmed it was pulling its funding of LIV at the end of 2026 but it was funded through the rest of the season. LIV released a statement saying it was looking for external investors to finance the series going forward. PGA Tour commissioner Brian Rolapp said the tour was thinking about pathways to reinstate LIV players .

May 2026: Rahm agreed to pay his outstanding DP World Tour penalties and ensure he remained eligible to play at the 2027 Ryder Cup. Elsewhere, US President Trump backed LIV Players to return to the PGA Tour .

DeChambeau said his future on the PGA Tour depended on whether players wanted him back , as speculation mounted over whether he would agree a new LIV Golf contract .

July 2026: Rahm said he was hopeful LIV Golf could continue but was tight-lipped on what the future would hold for the league.

August 2026: After much speculation, LIV Golf CEO O'Neil said the league had found a new lead investor , although was unable to provide details. The league also said players would become majority equity holders.

August 2026: LIV Golf finally confirmed its season-ending Team Championship in Michigan would no longer go ahead , following weeks of speculation, seeing the 2026 campaign finish a week early in Indianapolis.

September 2026: The league informed 'the majority of its workforce' that their employment under LIV 1.0 would end , having previously warned of redundancies earlier in the year.

September 2026: LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States but reiterated its intention to start a new version of the league, dubbed LIV 2.0, from 2027. Rahm and DeChambeau are listed as the players still owed the most.

October 2026: A representative for Rahm told a bankruptcy hearing that the Spaniard did not intend to participate in LIV 2.0 , with the 2023 Masters champion deeming the terms for the league's proposed relaunch to be "unacceptable".

Watch the PGA Tour, DP World Tour, majors and more throughout the season live on Sky Sports Golf. Get Sky Sports or stream with no contract on NOW .

articles.title: Tony Romo Disqualified from Korn Ferry Golf Qualifying Tournament After Scorecard Mix-Up
articles.summary: Former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo's latest attempt to play on the Korn Ferry Tour reportedly ended in a disqualification.
articles.body:
Former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo's latest attempt to play on the Korn Ferry Tour reportedly ended in a disqualification.

Michael Bamberger of Golf.com reported Romo played in a Korn Ferry pre-qualifier tournament at the Club at Forest Ridge in Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, earlier this month and was disqualified for signing an incorrect scorecard following his third round.

He had an opportunity to finish in the top 37 of the 54-hole tournament and advance to the first stage of the Korn Ferry Q-School after a solid first and second round. While he was officially disqualified, he also didn't play well enough in the third round to advance had the scorecard been correct.

Romo played his third round with college golfer Ethan Smith and professional Brandon Rice.

The former Cowboys star signed for a score of 74, although Rice also kept his score and thought Romo scored a five on the 16th hole despite signing for a score of four, per Bamberger.

Bamberger noted PGA Tour rules official Rob Keller said a South Central PGA pro also said Romo shot a five on the 16th hole and the 17th hole even though he signed for a score of four on each of them.

Signing for a lower score than was actually shot results in a disqualification if it is not fixed within 15 minutes, even if it is an honest mistake. Keller explained to Bamberger that Romo took responsibility and was "very complimentary" of the event.

Perhaps most notably, neither score would have been good enough to advance.

Last week, CBS Sports and Romo mutually parted ways , ending his broadcast career with the company. Steve Megargee of the Associated Press reported on Sept. 1 that Romo pleaded no contest to a charge of operating while intoxicated after he was arrested in July.

articles.title: Zack Polanski failed to show leadership over Zionism motion, ex-Green leader says
articles.summary: Caroline Lucas tells the BBC Zack Polanski should have taken part in a vote on a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.
articles.body:
Zack Polanski failed to show leadership over a motion passed by Green Party members declaring Zionism a form of racism, the party's former leader Caroline Lucas has told the BBC.

Lucas told Newsnight that the party's current leader, who did not attend the debate on the motion at the Green Party's annual conference in Brighton, "should have been there and he should have voted".

She described the motion, which defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state", as "dangerous" and "divisive".

In the wake of the vote, Polanski has said he will not accept anyone being excluded from the Green Party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of".

Lucas's comments came after polls closed in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, where Polanski is standing as a candidate.

Polanski did not vote on the motion after leaving the party's conference early to campaign in the north London constituency.

The Green leader has declined media interviews since the motion was passed on Sunday and did not answer questions from a BBC reporter about the motion earlier on Thursday.

The motion also backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

Lucas, who voted against the motion, said: "I would have hoped [Polanski] would have been a very strong critic of this motion."

She added that it was "flawed from top to bottom".

Asked if Polanski should stand down, she told Newsnight: "I think let's just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this by-election.

"I want him to speak now about what's happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday.

"I think the jury is out about whether he will do that - but I very much hope he will."

In response to Lucas's comments, a Green Party source said: "There are ups and downs in politics and when people are passionate they disagree in the heat of a campaign.

"We do things differently - unlike Labour who use anonymous sources and resort to factionalism."

The motion has overshadowed the final days of Polanski's by-election campaign, where the Greens have been looking to overturn a substantial Labour majority in the seat vacated by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer .

It has sparked days of controversy and exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general election.

Four of the five Green MPs opposed the motion, while the party's co-deputy leaders were split over whether they supported it.

The vote also led to the resignation of the Green deputy leader in Wales and condemnation from the European Green Party.

In a written statement on Monday, Polanski did not specify whether he supported the motion passed by members but sought to reassure Jewish members that "no-one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith, or where they worship".

Polanski, who is Jewish, added that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct".

Ahead of the vote, he had backed an amendment to specify that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist, but this was voted down by members.

He had also said he wanted to see the reference to a single Palestinian state changed, arguing: "I don't believe we as a Green Party of England and Wales, or even the British government, should be deciding what the future settlement looks like."

I won't accept exclusion within Green Party, says Polanski after criticism of Zionism motion

Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote

Polanski banned from Israel after party's motion declaring 'Zionism is racism'

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on Polanski to reverse the motion and ensure it is not Green Party policy.

In his first comment on the row, Burnham said it was "completely wrong" for the party to support the motion and this showed "terrible judgement".

The PM said he felt the motion effectively ruled out a two-state solution between Israel and Palestine.

"For that reason, it shouldn't be supported in any way, shape or form," he told reporters while on a visit to Berlin.

When asked if he would rule out entering into coalition with the Greens, he would not be drawn on "any business about what might or might not happen in the future".

On Thursday, a Green Party spokesperson said: "This has been an emotive issue and is complex. It has rightly caused much discussion, and needs to be taken in the context that Israel's behaviour has had.

"Israel has been responsible for a genocide, ethnic cleansing and the killing of children, and we've had a political establishment which has not only turned a blind eye but provided support."

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is currently hearing a case brought by South Africa that accuses Israeli forces of genocide, but it could take years to reach a conclusion. Israel has called the case "wholly unfounded" and based on "biased and false claims".

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Stark warning' over ADHD and 'Andrew wins legal fight'
articles.summary: A government review of ADHD and austism diagnoses and the police investigation into Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor lead Friday's papers.
articles.body:
This paper review contains spoilers from the third episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

The result of the Holborn and St Pancras by-election came too late for the printed editions of the papers, but the Guardian website says Zack Polanski "fell short" in the high-stakes battle for the left of British politics. The Daily Mail says Polanski suffered a "heavy defeat , " raising questions over his future as Green leader. The Daily Telegraph says he has vowed to stay on, despite being rejected by voters after the anti-Semitism row in his party. " Green with envy ," is The Sun's headline

The Daily Mail says the rush to diagnose autism can "damage children" - citing a report that warns that parents are being incentivised to have their children diagnosed, by misguided schools and welfare systems that reward such labels. The Times says the review warns that early diagnosis could close doors in adulthood. But the Guardian highlights the conclusion of Professor Peter Fonagy, who penned the review, that "the rise in mental health problems is real and cannot be explained by greater awareness alone ".

The Times says a prolific shoplifter who praised Andy Burnham as he walked out of prison under the government's early release scheme was sent back to jail within days, after going on a crime spree. The paper says the police spent 27 hours of their time bringing Michael Bogle back into custody. It quotes a letter from a local Metropolitan Police Commander as saying that the time could have been better spent "in the community, progressing other investigations or targeing high-harm offenders". The Sun says that a staggering 95% of prisoners who breached their tagging conditions on the scheme were simply bailed back into the community with "zero sanction" .

Many of the papers highlight the police admission that the warrants used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes in February were unlawful. The Sun notes that that police chiefs say their investigation into Andrew will continue at pace . "It's not over," agrees the Daily Mirror , which writes that the judge determined that the unlawful warrants do not invalidate the entire investigation. Mountbatten-Windsor denies any wrongdoing. The Daily Telegraph cites friends of Andrew saying his fightback starts now . Writing in The i Paper , the former BBC royal correspondent Jenny Bond says Mountbatten-Windsor will be rubbing his hands with glee that a rare bit of good news has come his way.

images.caption: Several of today's papers lead with the government's review of ADHD and autism diagnoses. A "stark warning over rising demand for NHS autism and ADHD care" tops the Guardian. Elsewhere, it reports that two Latvians have been arrested after they were "found inside RAF base". And, after it was revealed that the three sisters who died in the Brighton sea had taken their own lives, the paper describes their "final pilgrimage".

articles.title: Labour sees off Green challenge to win Holborn by-election
articles.summary: Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali beats Green Party leader Zack Polanski to hold the north London seat.
articles.body:
Labour has won the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, seeing off a challenge from Green Party leader Zack Polanski.

Camden council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali held the north London seat for Labour, but the party's majority was reduced from 11,572 to 3,364.

The by-election, which was triggered after former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer stood down as an MP, had been seen as a key test of whether Labour under Andy Burnham can win over voters who have switched to the Greens.

Polanski insisted he would stay on as leader despite the result.

He has also come under pressure over his response to a policy motion passed by members at his party's conference that declared Zionism a form of racism.

Labour wins Holborn and St Pancras by-election, beating Green leader Zack Polanski

Polanski defends leadership after Zionism row and by-election loss

Chris Mason: Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far

Labour's Abdi-Wali secured 45% of the vote, followed by Polanski on 33%.

However, the Green Party's vote share was up by 22% on the 2024 general election.

Ewan Cameron of the Conservatives came a distant third with 1,922 votes (7%), followed by Reform UK, the Liberal Democrats and Restore Britain.

The inner London constituency has been Labour since it was created in 1983, with the party taking at least 40% of the vote at every general election.

In her victory speech at the count in Camden, Abdi-Wali, who came to the UK as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a testament to the success of diversity in the borough.

"Whether you voted for me or not, my commitment to this community runs deep," she said.

"I hope this moment also says something about who gets to belong, for people who look like me, I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden, and this is Britain."

She added: "That is what this victory represents. Winning not by making people afraid of each other, but by bringing people together."

Asked what had gone wrong for his party, Polanski said his party had increased its vote share in the seat since the last election, describing the result as "our second best by-election result in Green Party history".

"I'm not going to sit here and pretend I'm not disappointed. No politician runs in a by-election and doesn't want to win," he told told BBC Radio 4's Today.

"But at the same time, to see the growth in what was supposedly a safe Labour seat since 1983 [and] is now a marginal Labour seat, that's clearly growth and next time we can get it over the line."

Speaking to broadcasters earlier in the day, Polanski dismissed suggestions his leadership was under threat, saying: "Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green Party."

He said voters had been "excited about our plans for rent controls, tackling the climate crisis and nationalising Thames Water".

He continued: "So many people told me on the doorstep, so they want to give Andy Burnham a chance [as prime minister].

"Well, he's got a chance now. Let's see what he does with it."

The Greens had hoped they could overturn Labour's substantial majority in the constituency after the party made gains in local elections in the area in May.

It saw a surge in support after Polanski took over as leader in September last year but in recent months polls suggest this has waned.

The by-election came after Polanski faced criticism for his response to a motion passed by members declaring Zionism a form of racism.

Earlier, former party leader Caroline Lucas told the BBC Polanski had failed to show leadership over the motion.

Speaking after polls closed but before the result of the by-election was announced, Lucas criticised Polanski for not taking part in the debate or voting on the motion at the Green Party's conference in Brighton on Sunday, describing the motion as "dangerous" and "divisive".

Asked if Polanski should stand down, she said: "I think let's just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this by-election.

"I want him to speak now about what's happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday.

"I think the jury is out about whether he will do that - but I very much hope he will."

The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Polanski was not present for the vote on the motion, after leaving the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras.

articles.title: ‘I just like to be the first in everything’: Pranavi Urs sets sights on Olympic medal
articles.summary: Bengaluru: Pranavi Urs has always seemed to have a liking for firsts.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Pranavi Urs has always seemed to have a liking for firsts. In 2025, the Mysuru pro became the first Indian woman to win an open-field professional tournament against male golfers when she triumphed at the IGPL Invitational in Mumbai. Last week in Japan, she added the biggest first of them all, becoming the first Indian woman to win an individual gold at the Asian Games.“I just like to be the first in everything,” Pranavi said during an interaction facilitated by SAI. “I find ways to put myself in situations where no one’s ever been before.” For someone who has repeatedly ventured into uncharted territory, the Asian Games gold was another opportunity to test herself.The three-shot lead she carried into the final round disappeared after a triple bogey on the third hole. But unlike three years ago in Hangzhou, Pranavi knew what it was like to be in a high-pressure situation. More importantly, she had prepared for it.The night before the final round, Pranavi and her psychologist had visualised different scenarios, including what could happen if things went wrong. When the triple bogey arrived, she recognised the situation and reminded herself that she had reached rock bottom.“I was like, you’ve got nothing to lose, you’re at rock bottom now. The worst thing has already happened, so it can’t get worse,” she said.That preparation allowed her to return to the process rather than focus on the outcome. Even on the final hole, when the gold was within touching distance, she was thinking about making sure she secured a medal rather than winning it.She changed from a six-iron to a seven-iron for her second shot after feeling the adrenaline rush. She was so locked into the moment that she did not even realise her final putt was for gold.“I thought it was like, make par and maybe force a playoff,” she said. “Little did I know that the last putt that I hit was putt to win.”Hence, there was no elaborate celebration. She did not know she had won. Now, however, the significance of the gold is beginning to sink in, as is the possibility of what it could lead to.Pranavi’s next first could come on the Ladies European Tour, where she has been knocking on the door of a maiden victory. She believes her game is ready and that it is now a matter of patience.“I’ve come close to winning a couple of times. It just shows that my game is there and it’s just a matter of time,” she said.Closer home, the Women’s Indian Open remains a childhood dream. A win on home soil, she feels, would be special in a way no other victory could match.But Pranavi is already looking beyond those targets. Asked what the next ‘first’ she wants to chase is, she said, “To win an Olympic medal or a Major!”For someone who has already broken barriers at the domestic level and the Asian Games, the ambition is clear: the next frontier is no longer India, but the global arenas of the sport.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Zack Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far
articles.summary: The Green leader faces pressure over his response to a party motion declaring Zionism a form of racism, as well as his by-election loss.
articles.body:
In the aftermath of a by-election, the focus is usually on the winner. Not this time.

Make no mistake, the new MP for Holborn and St Pancras in north London, Sagal Abdi-Wali, has quite the story to tell.

She arrived in the UK as a child refugee from Somalia in the 1990s, grew up locally in Camden, became a councillor four years ago, the council leader in May and is now Sir Keir Starmer's successor as the MP.

But in the offices of Camden Council at three o'clock this morning, the focus of the press pack, me included, was on Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green Party of England and Wales, as we waited for the result.

This constituency has long been a safe Labour seat – the political home of the former prime minister and before that the former cabinet minister Frank Dobson. So a Labour victory here falls in the column marked "relief" for Downing Street rather than "jubilation".

Nonetheless, the Greens did very well in local elections in London in May, riding the crest of a political wave which began shortly after Polanski became the party's leader just over a year ago.

His failure to win here will prompt questions from some about stalling momentum, but the party can and does point to the big swing to them since the general election and a result that was by a long way the second best ever result for them at a Westminster by-election.

Incidentally, in finishing third the Conservatives have beaten Reform UK for the first time in an English by-election since the general election. It seems likely that Reform's result was hampered by Restore Britain, who managed almost half as many votes as Reform did, in a constituency not very favourable to either party.

Follow live updates: Labour wins Holborn and St Pancras by-election, beating Green leader Zack Polanski

Polanski defends leadership after Zionism row and by-election loss

But the real reason for the nocturnal scramble of cameras, microphones and questions for Polanski had little to do with the by-election – and everything to do with a vote at the Green Party's conference in Brighton last weekend.

Activists there passed a motion declaring Zionism as a form of racism.

The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Polanski didn't take part in the vote because, he said, he chose to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras instead. And he repeatedly declined to do interviews, as the pressure on him as ratcheted up.

But this morning he did speak to journalists.

He told BBC Breakfast that if he had he been there for the vote he "would have voted for the amendments".

Asked if he would have voted against the motion in the hall on that day, Polanski said: "the motion as amended I would have voted for, the motion unamended I wouldn't have voted for."

He added: "I think it's an imperfect motion, there's parts I disagree with and parts I agree with."

Some in the party are furious about what has happened in recent days, with one figure telling me: "He has created a monster he either can't or won't control."

Green Party membership has increased more than three fold in the last year and internal critics of Polanski say this includes hard-left campaigners focused on the Middle East rather than environmental concerns.

Within the party and beyond it, a row is now boiling. Polanski, who is himself Jewish, has been banned from Israel. The Jewish Leadership Council and the Board of Deputies of British Jews have criticised the party, as have sister Green parties in Europe.

And – significantly – the former party leader and one of the most important figures in the Green movement of her generation, Caroline Lucas, told BBC Newsnight Polanski had failed to show leadership over the issue . She also failed to back him carrying on as leader.

Asked by reporters after the by-election result if he could continue as leader, Polanski insisted "of course I can carry on".

He did not explicitly reject the motion his party has passed, saying there was an "ongoing genocide and the displacement of the Palestinian people".

"I believe that is clearly racist," he added.

Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

And asked if he believed in a two-state solution – an Israeli and Palestinian state existing peacefully alongside each other – he said "I believe it is not our role to decide".

He repeated that "it is my job to reassure people and make sure that we bring our party together".

"No one will be excluded in the Green Party based on faith and religion," he said.

But Polanski now confronts the greatest crisis of his leadership so far. He faces open, public insurrection about his judgement from senior figures internally and opprobrium from plenty of others beyond the party.

The campaign in Holborn and St Pancras might be over. The questions for Polanski certainly aren't.

articles.title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu to Indians who are on a visa in US: Come back; America no longer …

articles.body: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has urged Indians living and working in the US on a visa to return to India, saying many Indians who have contributed to America's technology sector are now facing uncertainty about their future there. In a post on X (formerly known as Twitter), Sridhar Vembu said that Indians had played a major role in building America's technological strength, but added that a section of the country no longer wanted them. “Indians have made a major contribution to America's technological prowess. Yet, a big part of America no longer wants us,” Vembu wrote.He also highlighted the personal cost of immigration uncertainty for Indians who have built their lives in the US after years of hard work. “Indians who are on a visa in the US face the painful prospect of uprooting the life you have built with hard work,” he said.“Let this be the birth pains of a bold new future. Come back, let's build India 🙏,” he wrote.Sridhar Vembu's comments come amid concerns among Indian professionals about their ability to work and settle in the US. Many Indian technology workers depend on employment-based visas, including the H-1B visa, while some seek permanent residency through the Green Card process.When a user asked “What exactly was the problem with India, that the brains from India built US whereas they could not do anything here”, Vembu replied:“The Chinese migrated in large numbers even as China developed.Taiwanese migrated in large numbers as Taiwan developed. Same with South Korea and before that Japan.My point is that development at a national level accompanies out migration of talent seeking better opportunities faster”.Sridhar Vembu wrote an open letter to Indians in AmericaIn April this year, Vembu shared an open letter addressed to Indians living in the United States. The letter then urged “brothers and sisters from Bharat” to consider returning to India and contribute to the country’s growth. In the post, Vembu reflected on his own journey to the US decades ago and acknowledged the opportunities it provided. At the same time, he pointed to changing perceptions around immigration and jobs, saying that Indians abroad are increasingly caught in broader political debates.“You may think the next election will fix this, but your choice would be between people who hate our Bharatiya civilisation and people who hate civilisation itself. articles.title: The Celtic Board’s Defensive Smokescreen Against Modernisation
articles.summary: A Peek Behind The Curtain – Decoding “Coercion”: The Celtic Board’s defensive smokescreen against modernisation. It’s the latest hard-hitting column from Col...
articles.body:
A Peek Behind The Curtain – Decoding "Coercion": The Celtic Board's defensive smokescreen against modernisation. It's the latest hard-hitting column from Colin Dempster…

The Alfred Dunhill Links Championship at The Old Course, St Andrews, Scotland on 03 October 2026: Celtic majority shareholder Dermot Desmond on the 18th green at the Old Course, St Andrews Photo Alex Todd IMAGO

£66 million cash reserve used as a shield against ambition

With a £66 million cash reserve used as a shield against ambition, the boardroom's attack on fans exposes an autocratic regime desperately fighting to protect its monopoly on power.

If you spend enough time watching the administrative machinery of modern football, you start to realise it isn't built to be dynamic; it's built to endure. It's reinforced with corporate concrete, coated in PR gloss, and designed to absorb shock.

A bad weekend on the pitch? Absorb it. A wave of anger on social media? Let it break against the barrier and wait for the tide to recede.

13th September 2026; Ibrox. Scottish League Cup Football, Rangers versus Celtic; Rangers players applaud their fans as the scoreboard reads Rangers 3 Celtic 0. Photo Vagelis Georgariou

For years, the standard playbook for the fanbase was the loud, emotional outburst — a roar of frustration that echoed through the stands for ninety minutes and then evaporated into the Glasgow air by Monday morning.

The administration knew exactly how to handle that. They've built soundproofing into the windows and learned how to wait out the storm.

Tennis balls on the Old Course at St Andrews as Celtic fans protest against Dermot Desmond's running of the football club. Photo via Conor Spence

It starts to look a lot like The Shawshank Redemption. On one side, you have Dermot Desmond playing the part of the warden—sitting comfortably behind institutional walls, pulling the strings from a distance, believing his authority is absolute, and assuming the supporters will eventually quiet down and fall in line.

On the other side, you have the Celtic supporters, tired of being managed, realising that no amount of shouting at the Governor's office is going to unlock the doors.

Nothing exposed this warden-and-prisoner dynamic more clearly than the board's recent panic over the official Celtic Football Club statement.

Dermot Desmond's quiet afternoon on a golf green

For months, a parallel, highly structured network of independent supporter organisations has been pointing out major operational bottlenecks. Yet the moment a few symbolic tennis balls disrupted the principal shareholder's quiet afternoon on a golf green, the machinery found its voice, unleashing a furious corporate broadside.

Alfred Dunhill Links Championship Dermot Desmond walks off the 18th green with a close security guard. Alfred Dunhill Links Championship, Golf, Round 3, Old Course St Andrews, Scotland, Photo Stuart Wallace/Shutterstock IMAGO

The language used was a classic piece of institutional engineering: the board claimed they would not be "coerced" or "intimidated" by organised supporter groups.

Let's clear the tracks right away: when an autocratic management screams about "coercion," it is a deliberate rhetorical smoke screen. They are perfectly comfortable with passive disagreement — fans venting on phone-in radio shows or buying tickets while grumbling under their breath.

What they cannot tolerate is coordinated leverage that bypasses their clinical corporate communications apparatus.

To the boardroom, forcing a direct confrontation where their PR buffers can't protect them feels like extortion. It is simply the only language an unyielding infrastructure understands when every official channel has been intentionally designed as a dead end.

Alfred Dunhill Links Championship Dermot Desmond walks off the 18th green with a close security guard. Alfred Dunhill Links Championship, Golf, Round 3, Old Course St Andrews, Scotland, Photo Stuart Wallace

The supreme irony is that the fans are not asking to burn the stadium down; they are asking for basic, structural modernisation. Supporters want to drag the club's operations out of the early 2000s and replace outdated internal compromises with world-class, elite European standards.

They want a fully empowered Director of Football commanding an independent, data-driven recruitment system, rather than an archaic scouting setup reliant on boardroom networks, alongside top class coaching at all levels.

They want genuine democratic accountability alongside a decent match going or online experience all perfectly achievable within the club's current finances.

Alfred Dunhill Links Championship Dermot Desmond is driven away from the Old Course after finishing his 3rd round with a close security guard in the front seat of the golf buggy, Old Course St Andrews on 03 October 2026. Photo Stuart Wallace Shutterstock/ IMAGO

True progress means giving up absolute control

But the board is intentionally blocking these changes. They aren't rejecting modernisation out of laziness; they are doing it because true progress means giving up absolute control.

In a modern football club, a billionaire shareholder or a legacy chairman cannot personally veto a transfer or pick a manager based on pure gut feeling. Professionalising the club means handing the keys over to independent specialists.

For men who have spent decades running the club as their private fiefdom, giving up that power is unthinkable. Stagnation is their protective shield. We see it laid bare in the club's own annual financial accounts: the board is perfectly content sitting on a massive cash reserve of over £66 million, viewing it as a buffer of comfort rather than a tool for ambition.

They tolerate a massive 22% drop in revenue and a slide into an on-paper financial loss because missing out on the Champions League phase is an acceptable cost to them, so long as the domestic status quo remains insulated.

They don't want a modern, dynamic club because a modern club belongs to the people who care about the football, whereas a stagnant, insulated club belongs entirely to the boardroom.

Celtic v theRangers – Scottish Premiership – Celtic Supporters hold up a Let Celtic Flourish banner during the match at Celtic Park on Sunday September 1, 2024. Photo Steve Welsh

We as Celtic supporters are forever on at the board for their staggering inability to learn lessons. Year after year, we watch them make the same structural blunders in Europe, repeat the same recruitment failures, and hide behind the same tired excuses.

But if we are going to demand that they learn, we must be honest enough to look in the mirror and learn our own lessons first. In this fight against institutional stagnation, emotional knee-jerks are no longer fit for purpose.

Jimmy Reid's historic Upper Clyde Shipbuilders speeches

We need to look back at the finest traditions of this city's working-class struggle to find our blueprint. Go back to Jimmy Reid's historic Upper Clyde Shipbuilders speeches. When the workers took control, Reid didn't call for a wild, chaotic riot; he demanded absolute tactical discipline.

He told the men that unity was their only shield, warning them that the establishment was actively waiting for the first sign of trouble, the first broken window, or the first piece of anti-social behaviour to weaponise it and smash their movement.

The exact same logic applies to us today. The Celtic boardroom and their well-compensated PR gatekeepers are sitting behind their corporate concrete, watches synchronised, desperately waiting for the fanbase to slip up.

The absolute second an online campaign crosses the line, or an in-person protest descends into undisciplined chaos, they will pounce. They will use it to paint the entire Celtic Fans Collective as a fringe group of lawless agitators, completely vindicating their narrative of "coercion" to the wider public.

Celtic supporters at Fir Park. Photographs by Vagelis Georgariou

We cannot give them that leverage. If we break ranks, if we let frustration turn into a chaotic rabble, we lose. Unity and iron-clad discipline are the only tools that can protect this movement.

We must become a highly organised, immovable front that handles its business with clinical precision. That is how you turn a wave of raw anger into a functional tool.

When you start reacting out of pure frustration, you think a single, well-crafted argument is going to make the penny drop and change everything overnight. Then you realise institutions don't work like that. They don't have epiphanies; they have compliance departments.

To truly challenge that kind of control, you must change how you fight. You stop swinging for the fences with short-lived outbursts and you pick up the hammer.

Freedom doesn't come from a single dramatic moment; it comes from consistent, unvarnished, systemic analysis aimed straight at the root causes of institutional stagnation. No emotional knee-jerks, no corporate spin, just the steady sound of a tiny rock hammer chipping away at a massive institutional wall, day after day, until the narrative belongs to the supporters again.

Let Dermot Desmond and his appointed wardens keep their guarded corridors and their closed-door meetings.

The wall doesn't need to come down in one loud crash, it just needs enough steady, patient pressure until the light finally starts to get through. They can say they don't recognise the Celtic Fans Collective, but they can't ignore the vast numbers of Celtic fans signing up.

But the fans on the streets of Glasgow cannot swing the hammer alone. The strength of this club has never been confined to the parameters of the East End; it lives in the lungs of a massive, global community. From Boston to Brisbane, New York to Toronto, our identity was forged by an immigrant diaspora that understood the absolute necessity of collective solidarity.

A battle to reclaim the soul of OUR football club

Now, the modern front line of that heritage is the Celtic Fans Collective . It is time for every supporter's club, every international enclave, and every member of the worldwide Celtic diaspora to actively stand up, join the Celtic Fans Collective , and get in this fight.

This is no longer just about ninety minutes on a match day. It is a battle to reclaim the soul of OUR football club. Stand disciplined, stand together, and let's start chipping away at the wall.

For more on the Celtic Fans Collective watch this…

articles.title: Forest Green Rovers sign free agent defender McIntyre
articles.summary: Forest Green Rovers sign centre-back Tom McIntyre on a short-term contract.
articles.body:
Forest Green Rovers have signed central defender Tom McIntyre on a short-term contract.

The 27-year-old former Scotland youth international has agreed a deal until next January.

He most-recently had a short spell at Scottish top-flight side Aberdeen, where he made five appearances late last season.

He came through the ranks at Reading, playing more than 100 games in the Championship and League One before joining Portsmouth in the summer of 2024.

McIntyre made 14 appearances for Pompey before joining Aberdeen at the end of this year's winter transfer window having also had loan spells at Charlton Athletic and Bradford City.

"Having worked with Tom during my time at Reading, I know the qualities he can bring to the team with his extensive EFL experience, leadership qualities and undoubted ability," Forest green director of football Mark Bowen told the club website.

articles.title: Readers weigh in on Alabama football vs Georgia | Goodbread mailbag
articles.summary: Readers of The Tuscaloosa News weigh in with their thoughts and questions about Alabama football's weekend clash with Georgia.
articles.body:
There won't be a more anticipated game in college football Saturday, Oct. 10 than Alabama-Georgia , a top-10 matchup that will have the nation's attention (6:30 p.m. CT, ABC). It will be the fourth time the rivals have met since UA coach Kalen DeBoer's arrival in 2024. The Crimson Tide has taken two of the three, but was drummed by the Bulldogs in the SEC title game last December. Here are some questions and thoughts about the game from the Sounding Board (email below to join), a group of Tuscaloosa News readers who participate in the occasional mailbag column.

Derek from Indianapolis writes : There has been a noticeable difference in preparation, attention to detail, development and execution this year. The coaches would say there always has been, but this year it's actually coming to fruition. What would you contribute that to?

Hey Derek : I would identify two factors here; one, the maturity of the transfer class. That's not a given from year to year, and in fact, it's often lacking. This group places team success at a high priority. Secondly, there is every indication coach Kalen DeBoer hit home runs with his offseason coaching hires, most of which were on the offensive side. The most impactful of those have been offensive line coach Adrian Klemm and tight ends coach Richard Owens, who've made a transformational impact at their respective positions.

Monte from Brooklyn writes : Am I wrong to think that the secondary has not lived up to its preseason billing? Do you think they can get better?

Hey Monte : Notwithstanding some ugly hiccups against Florida State , I'd mostly disagree. The starters — Zabien Brown, Dijon Lee, Bray Hubbard, Keon Sabb and Red Morgan — have given up some big pass plays but have also been opportunistic with turnovers. There is also some stellar depth developing rather quickly.

Jeff from Montgomery writes : What's the next step in Keelon Russell's development as a quarterback? He already seems so polished.

Hey Jeff : It's getting hard to pick nits with Russell's game now that he's cleaned up early-season issues with ball security and self-preservation (he's now finishing runs with a slide). His pocket awareness is improving by the week, which is leading to smarter decisions and more explosive plays. He'll still hold the ball too long on occasion, but he's been nothing short of elite as a passer.

Samantha from Atlanta writes : What has been the biggest difference in the improvement of the pass rush this year?

Hey Samantha : Devan Thompkins, to be frank, has been better than I expected, and is on a pace to have a far more productive season than he did at Southern Cal a year ago. He's not the only reason the pass rush is better, but what it needed was a Robin to Yhonzae Pierre's Batman, and Thompkins has been just that. Pockets are shrinking from the interior, owing largely to Thompkins, Terrence Green, London Simmons and others.

Drew from Mobile writes : When will EJ Crowell take on a bigger role in the running back rotation?

Hey Drew : It could happen as early as the Georgia game, if offensive coordinator Ryan Grubb's Monday remarks are telling. I wrote about this earlier in the week ; the freshman is still learning the offense, but he's also too good to keep under wraps.

Tuscaloosa News columnist Chase Goodbread is also the weekly co-host of Crimson Cover TV on WVUA-23. Reach him at cgoodbread@gannett.com. Follow on X.com @chasegoodbread.

articles.title: Zack Polanski vows to stay as Green leader as he faces criticism after by-election defeat
articles.summary: Jewish Greens' leader has said Polanski should resign in the wake of a Zionism row and by-election defeat.
articles.body:
Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Green Party leader after his by-election defeat, as he faced pressure from within his own party to resign.

The leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, said on Friday he should resign, adding it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.

Lichtenstein's comments come after two former Green leaders accused Polanski of failing to show leadership over the Zionism row.

Polanski, who came second to Labour overnight in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and "of course" had not questioned that.

The Greens had hoped to take the seat, previously held by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, after a by-election success earlier this year .

Polanski lost out in Thursday's contest in London to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22 percentage points on the 2024 general election.

In her comments calling on Polanski to resign, Lichtenstein told Times Radio: "I don't know which Jewish members of the party he's been working with – it certainly hasn't been with the Jewish Greens committee."

Her criticisms were similar to those of former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas who said Polanski should have attended the vote on the conference motion on Sunday.

The motion, which was passed by rank-and-file members to become official party policy, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Adrian Ramsay, a Green MP and former co-leader, declined to back Polanski when asked on the BBC's Politics East on Friday.

"A lot depends on what happens in the days and weeks to come," he replied when asked if Polanski should still lead the party.

"[He] did not show leadership I would have been looking for," said Ramsay, who said he was now working to reverse the motion.

Polanski defended his absence from the controversial motion vote in Brighton, saying he was busy campaigning in the North London constituency.

Asked if he would resign, he said: "Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green Party."

He added: "Yes, I've taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion."

Having not answered questions about the Zionism vote for most of this week, Polanski confirmed in interviews on Friday that he would not have voted for the "imperfect" motion without it being amended.

However, he said "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology".

Several UN reports have accused the Israeli government of committing war crimes which amount to genocide in Gaza. Israel has repeatedly denied all such allegations.

On Friday morning, following the Zionism row, Polanski was asked repeatedly on BBC Radio 4's Today programme whether he believes Israel has a right to exist.

"I don't believe any state has the right to oppress or to commit apartheid and certainly not genocide on another people," he said, adding: "I don't believe that's a state that anyone should be supporting."

Asked by presenter Nick Robinson for a "yes/no" answer on this question, he said: "I've repeated many times that I want to see equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - at the moment Palestinians don't have equal rights so I think I'm answering your question really clearly."

In private, plenty of longstanding Green figures remain frustrated and accuse Polanski of being "missing in action" over the motion.

They say the result is an untenable situation where he leads a party whose policy on the Middle East he disagrees with.

"He is in danger of losing the confidence of both wings," one critic pointed out, referring to how some supporters of the motion have now been left irritated too by Polanski's refusal to publicly back them.

Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far

Labour sees off Green challenge to win Holborn by-election

But given his popularity among the grassroots, he may be safe from a leadership challenge in the near future.

Former Green leader Caroline Lucas described the motion as "dangerous" and "flawed from top to bottom", and said leadership "was frankly missing" on it.

She said she was not calling for Polanski to stand down and welcomed that he had "indicated he shares some of my concerns on the Zionism motion".

"Now the party needs to come together to make the urgent changes needed to take us forward," she said.

Jonathan Bartley, the Green co-leader from 2016 to 2021, called on Polanski to "put his hands up" and "say sorry" - but did not demand he quit.

"I think [the vote] was a failure of leadership from Zack and there is a certain toxicity now around the Green Party," he told BBC Radio 4's World at One.

Bartley said the Green brand "needs to be detoxified", adding the party had seen an influx in members that have "maybe come from the left of the Labour Party, maybe from [Jeremy Corbyn's] Your Party" but "we're losing some older voters".

The party's next scheduled leadership ballot takes place in summer 2027 - and Bartley said he thinks Polanski will face a challenger.

Sian Berry, Green MP for Brighton Pavilion, said on Friday she was ready to work with colleagues "to restore trust in our processes and our party, fix the serious flaws in the motion that was passed" and build more inclusive policies.

The Green leader has faced days of pressure over the Zionism motion. Four of the five Green MPs and one of the party's two deputy leaders opposed it, the Green deputy in Wales and some councillors resigned, while some local members and the European Green Party have distanced themselves from it.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on Polanski to reverse the "completely wrong" motion.

Meanwhile, Labour chair Bridget Phillipson drew comparisons with her party's previous antisemitism scandal , telling the BBC she felt the Greens now face a "serious problem" with antisemitism.

Polanski has said anti-Zionism and antisemitism are distinct from each other and said nobody will be excluded from the party on the basis of their faith, place of worship or religious body.

articles.title: Labour fends off the Green party in closely watched UK by-election
articles.summary: Sagal Abdi-Wali won by 3,300 votes in the London seat of Holborn and St Pancras.
articles.body:
The Labour Party has won an election for a parliamentary seat vacated by former leader Keir Starmer, fending off a challenge from the left-wing Green Party in a boost for the British prime minister.

Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali , the leader of the local council, won the seat in the central London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras with 12,292 votes, compared with 8,928 for Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader who came second.

The victory, which had been expected, will buoy Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was recently installed by lawmakers fearful that Starmer’s unpopularity was opening the way for a challenge by the populist Reform UK party at the next national election.

After losing left-wing support to the Greens earlier this year, Labour looks to have won many voters back, a result that triggered more questions about Polanski’s leadership.

There are now five Green MPs, compared with one in 2023.

But Polanski, 43, recently came under fire after party members passed a motion declaring that Zionism is racism at their annual conference.

The move, which called for “the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine” was criticised by Jewish groups, other parties and most Green Party lawmakers. Polanski did not vote on the motion.

Labour has held Holborn since the seat was created in 1983.

Labour’s Abdi-Wali, who arrived in the United Kingdom as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a defeat for “those who seek to divide us”.

“We have a responsibility to defend what we’ve built and pass it on,” she said.

After conceding defeat, Polanski, who is not an MP, answered his critics, saying he would stay on as leader, and described the result as part of “Andy Burnham’s honeymoon”.

Polanski congratulated Abdi-Wali, but said, “One in three voters backed us here, and we know that many more considered it.”

Al Jazeera’s Sonia Gallego, reporting from London, said, “The constituency has been going through what some people have been calling ‘ the Burnham bounce ‘ … so far there is a deep sigh of relief (among Labour) that they’ve managed to hold on.”

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has changed voter habits during the past three years. The Greens, far more critical of Israel’s conduct than any other party, got a boost in the 2024 general election.

Back then, Starmer won the seat with 49 percent. Andrew Feinstein, a pro-Palestine independent candidate, came second, with 19 percent.

Polanski has raised the “progressive vote” while “reducing the Labour vote”, Feinstein said.

articles.title: Sergio García se despide de los Fireballs mientras lucha en el Open de España
articles.standfirst: El castellonense firma el par hoy y se mantiene arriba, aunque con la sensación de que pudo haber logrado un resultado mucho mejor
articles.summary: El castellonense firma el par hoy y se mantiene arriba, aunque con la sensación de que pudo haber logrado un resultado mucho mejor
articles.body: LIV Golf ya es historia para Sergio García tras obtener la libertad contractual el jueves y se podría decir que una nueva etapa de su carrera ha arrancado en este Open de España presented by Madrid. El castellonense está logrando trasladar a este torneo las buenas sensaciones que transmitió el mes pasado en el European Masters y el Open de Irlanda. Aunque hoy haya cerrado la jornada firmando el par (71), su juego dice otra cosa. Está con 138 golpes en el total y el liderato provisional el escocés Grant Forrest tras hacer 67 (133 en el acumulado) en la sesión matinal, en la que Josele Ballester tiró 69 y con 140 mantiene opciones de cara al fin de semana. El rendimiento general del ganador del Masters 2017 y su feeling con el juego corto está siendo muy bueno, aunque por desgracia no le está sacando partido. No estuvo mal desde el tee y casi impecable con los hierros, pero se le escaparon varias opciones de birdie en los primeros nueve. García sentó cátedra desde los bunkers –casi emboca en el 16 o el 1- pero faltó rematar con el putt en algunos hoyos. El tripateo del 4 fue muy doloroso porque allí el jueves firmó un eagle. Su buen juego no le libró de fallos puntuales que sin embargo pagó muy caros. De tee a green estuvo sólido y ese es el camino, pero sábado será de obligado cumplimiento una ronda baja para pelear por el Open el domingo. En el tramo final volvió a ganarse algunas opciones de birdie que no pudo certificar hasta que en el hoyo 7 sacó a relucir sus ‘spanish hands’ y casi emboca desde el rough para eagle. Sin embargo, en el 8 calculó mal el segundo tiro y terminó con un bogey. En cualquier caso, Sergio es ya un jugador sin ataduras y enfocado en recuperar su sitio en el DP World Tour y en el equipo europeo de la Ryder Cup. El de Borriol ya no lucía hoy en el polo ni en su gorra distintivos de LIV Golf ni de su equipo, los Fireballs, y en su lugar luce el de su canal de Youtube. Sobre todo lo que rodea a LIV Golf, García apuntó tras finalizar su vuelta: “Ya soy agente libre, el logo de la gorra es de mi canal de Youtube. Estoy contento, ahora puedo empezar al futuro más suelto, con más opciones y a ver qué soy capaz de conseguir de aquí a que empiece la temporada. […] Sobre LIV 2.0 no hemos tomado ninguna decisión ahora mismo. Estoy agradecido, han sido cuatro años muy bonitos con David, Josele, Abraham, Carlos Ortiz, Eugenio, hemos disfrutado mucho. Si sigue para adelante LIV, veremos a ver qué ocurre. Si estoy yo, bien, y si no desearles lo mejor. […] Los jugadores podemos decir cosas que se pueden mejorar, pero las decisiones las toman los que mandan”. Respecto a su vuelta y sus opciones de cara al fin de semana, comentó: “Hay que pelear y luchar, sigo ahí todavía. El rough está complicado, muy denso y hoy he cogido más del que me habría gustado. Si se te queda la bola hundida no sabes cómo te saldrá. El par no es una vuelta mala, pero me habría gustado hacer menos. Podría haber jugado mejor, pero el bogey del 4 ha dolido. ¿El fin de semana? Yo lo que tengo que hacer es jugar lo mejor posibles y hacer el sábado -6 o -7”.

articles.title: “They Gonna Fire Him”: Shannon Sharpe Predicts Harsh Punishment for Stadium Worker Who Called Dak Prescott “Embarrassing”
articles.summary: The Dallas Cowboys were beaten 24-16 in their clash against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Thursday, but it wasn’t just the problems on the field that needed ta...
articles.body:
The Dallas Cowboys were beaten 24-16 in their clash against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Thursday, but it wasn't just the problems on the field that needed tackling. An incident off the field starring Dak Prescott has drawn a lot of attention.

Dak Prescott, who was jeered by fans after a tough outing, was walking in the back before an AT&T Stadium employee appeared to use the word "embarrassing". The incident went viral online, but analyst Shannon Sharpe had some tough predictions to make for the employee.

"That gonna cost a better job. You know they gonna fire him", Shannon Sharpe said about the employee.

"He probably making a minimum, he probably making $10-12 an hour…them fans they get so invested man, they feel they out there playing."

Dak Prescott Reacted to the Incident Later

Dak Prescott addressed the incident in front of media after the game, laying down his version of what happened.

"When he said it, I just happened to look at him, and at that point, he looked away," Prescott said. "And when I turned my head back, he said something else.

"And so that's the part that, just as a man or as just a person, feel free to speak your mind — just speak it. Don't cower away from the reaction that you're going to get.

"And so, if you're saying it's embarrassing, say it's embarrassing," he continued. "If you're saying it to me, then say it to me. Don't go back on it. So that's all that was, and hate that it's even being talked about, to be honest with you."

Prescott and the Cowboys will be back in action on Oct. 18 against the Green Bay Packers.

articles.body:
The Dallas Cowboys are off to a difficult start after falling to 2-3. With the team under pressure, the front office must decide how to improve the roster before the season slips away.

Owner Jerry Jones , however, made it clear that the Cowboys are still open to trades. He said he would spend future draft picks on a player with long-term potential, and Dallas is not giving up on this season.

Cowboys owner addresses future draft capital amid slow start

The Cowboys fell to 2-3 on Thursday night with a 24-16 home loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, who played without injured quarterback Baker Mayfield. Dallas had just beaten the Houston Texans 34-30 in Week 4 to get back to .500. Tampa Bay took control in the second half when their ground game wore down the Cowboys' defense to secure the lead.

After the loss, Jones was asked if one player is worth giving up future draft capital. "Yes, I wouldn't give up future capital for a player who didn't have some future or potential future," Jones said . "But would that make an impact this year? I'm just saying because the future capital that you have are draft picks and those guys have question marks with them too."

Jones expressed he was extraordinarily disappointed and surprised by how well Tampa Bay ran the ball, but Dallas is not quitting on the season. He added, "And so if we do see an opportunity and it fits for us, then we'll take a good look at it. No, I'm not, this isn't fold the tents here. We are two and three."

Dallas also played without cornerback Joey Porter Jr., its newest trade acquisition, due to an illness.

Jerry Jones refuses to fold the tents on the Cowboys season

Porter's arrival serves as the prime example of Jones' willingness to part with future assets, costing Dallas a 2028 second-round selection and a conditional 2027 sixth-round pick. The sixth-round pick is tied to a clause that reportedly sends it to Pittsburgh only if Porter is on the gameday roster for at least two games this season.

Jones also admitted Dallas did not see this start coming. "We didn't expect to be two and three. We didn't expect this, we didn't expect this Tampa team to come in here either," Jones said . "And they've got a lot of good players and they unquestionably, they were the better team."

Dallas next plays October 18 at Green Bay after a nine-day gap, and Porter is still waiting to give the Cowboys a return on that trade after missing the Tampa Bay game with an illness. He has appeared in one game for Dallas, the win over Houston.

articles.title: Chacarra comanda a la ‘Armada’ en el Open de España con Ayora a su estela
articles.standfirst: Los dos jóvenes jugadores españoles siguen arriba en el Abierto nacional
articles.summary: Los dos jóvenes jugadores españoles siguen arriba en el Abierto nacional
articles.body: Que el capitán del equipo europeo de la Ryder Cup convocara al madrileño Eugenio Chacarra (26 años) y al marbellí Ángel Ayora (21 años) para formar parte una concentración en Adare Manor hace unas semanas, estaba bien meditado. Luke Donald ve un potencial excepcional en estos dos jóvenes y ellos están demostrando con hechos que están llamados a hacer cosas importantes. Chacarra es a día de hoy un jugador más hecho y experimentado, con cinco victorias profesionales y tercer clasificado de la Race to Dubai; Ayora pelea por un primer triunfo que le otorgue ese plus de confianza tan necesario para los deportistas. Al inicio de la tarde todos estaban pendientes de si Eugenio, colíder tras el primer día, estaría en condiciones de jugar. No había asegurado que fuera a seguir en el torneo tras hacerse el jueves daño en el dedo del pie que se rompió hace unos días. Pese a lo incómodo de la situación, Chacarra compitió y sacó un buen resultado. Sin duda, tanto él como Ayora fueron la principal atracción de la sesión vespertina del Open de España presented by Madrid. El madrileño firmó 69 golpes y computa 135, mientras que el andaluz hizo 70 golpes para un total de 137. A ellos se une un destacado Sergio García (138), los tres a la estela del líder, el escocés Grant Forrest (133), quien en su día fue un destacado jugador universitario y al que recordamos por ganar a Jon Rahm su primer torneo universitario en formato stroke play. De los primeros nueve hoyos Eugenio salió al par. Estuvo más fuera de posición de lo habitual y si hubiera tenido su juego habitual de tee a green habría salido otra ronda. “Soy un buen ball-striking y no lo estamos pudiendo ver esta semana por lo del pie. Me han tratado para mitigar el dolor y no siento los dedos y eso influye en mi swing, sobre todo cuando uso el driver”, confesó. La confianza en su drive no está siendo la misma debido al problema en su pie derecho, pero se manejó muy bien con el putter y sólo se le vio algo más impreciso al inicio de los segundos nueve hoyos. El sino de su vuelta cambió por completo al enlazar birdies al 14 y 15, este último gracias a un putt extraordinario. Se anotó otro birdie en el 17 y en el 18 lo rozó y terminó con un gran sabor de boca la jornada. Por su parte, Ayora mostró una versión muy sólida en la primera parte del recorrido y perdió algo de control al final. El malagueño mereció salir de los primeros nueve hoyos con un puñado de birdies en su tarjeta, pero sólo anotó dos, más un bogey en el 8 –hizo birdie el jueves- debido a un tripateo. Ángel siguió dándose oportunidades, pero ya menos preciso desde tee, y el premio no llegó hasta el 14. En el 17 hizo una muy mala salida y se tradujo en otro bogey. Ayora dejó sus impresiones al terminar y se lamentó por no aprovechar su buen arranque: “Me sabe a poco el resultado de los primeros nueve hoyos porque estuve muy ordenado, pero perdoné con el putt. Después de los segundos nueve hoyos he fallado más desde el tee. […] De cara al fin de semana cuatro golpes de ventaja [del líder] es muy poco, sobre todo en este campo, donde no coger calle marca la diferencia”. En cualquier caso, el andaluz se ve bien posicionado: “Sí, antes del torneo habría firmado llegar así al fin de semana porque venía un poco regular desde el tee y ahora estoy mejor y este campo eso es fundamental”. Una de las buenas noticias para el golf europeo esta semana es el buen rendimiento Francesco Molinari (138), ganador del British Open en 2018, que pelea por volver a la senda victoriosa. Josele Ballester (140), otra de las jóvenes promesas de la ‘Armada’, tampoco ha dicho su última palabra. Después de dos días hay diez españoles que están bajo par... y eso da muchas opciones de triunfo; sólo siete fallaron el corte y lo pasaron 13. Shane Lowry y Ludvig Aberg están en 141 en el acumulado y pasan el corte, no así Justin Rose y Patrick Reed, ambos con 144, ni Bubba Watson con 145.
