articles.title: Jeff Bezos is putting $100 million into neglected city land; eight US cities will turn abandoned spaces into parks and wildlife habitats
articles.summary: Jeff Bezos is putting $100 million into neglected urban land across eight American cities, funding plans to turn vacant plots, former industrial sites and
articles.body: Jeff Bezos is putting $100 million into neglected urban land across eight American cities, funding plans to turn vacant plots, former industrial sites and unused spaces into public parks and wildlife habitats. As reported by Bezos Earth Fund, announced on 7 July 2026, the investment will support projects ranging from the restoration of 600 vacant properties in Cleveland to a new park on a former motorway ramp in Little Rock. Other plans include planting trees along a popular Salt Lake City trail, restoring wetlands in Indianapolis and expanding green space around Los Angeles’ historic Watts Towers. The projects are designed to improve access to nature while giving overlooked land a new purpose.Jeff Bezos’ $100 million investment targets vacant land in eight US citiesThe investment, announced on 7 July 2026, forms part of the Bezos Earth Fund's Greening America's Cities programme. The eight recipients are Allentown in Pennsylvania, Atlanta, Cleveland, Indianapolis, Little Rock in Arkansas, Los Angeles, Salt Lake City and Sioux Falls in South Dakota.The projects differ in scale and purpose. Some focus on bringing shade and play areas to neighbourhoods with limited access to green space. Others involve restoring wetlands, creating new walking routes or turning vacant properties into small natural areas scattered throughout residential districts. Native plants and trees will feature across the programme, alongside facilities for recreation and community activities.Reportedly, the latest announcement is the second round of funding under the programme. With the new investment, the Bezos Earth Fund says it has committed $150 million across 11 cities, working towards a wider goal of investing $400 million in urban green spaces across the United States.8 US cities will get Jeff Bezos’ $100 million for new parksCleveland, United StatesIndianapolis, United StatesSalt Lake City, United StatesLos Angeles, United StatesLittle Rock, United StatesAllentown, United StatesAtlanta, United StatesSioux Falls, United StatesJeff Bezos’ $100 million investment across US citiesCleveland plans to transform 600 vacant propertiesCleveland's project will address a large concentration of vacant land in the city's Hough and St. Clair-Superior neighbourhoods. Together, the areas are home to around 17,000 people and have experienced decades of underinvestment, leaving them with extensive empty plots, limited tree cover and significant health challenges.More than half of the parcels in these neighbourhoods are vacant, according to the project announcement. Rather than concentrating the investment on a single large park, the initiative will convert 600 publicly owned properties into a network of green spaces distributed across residential blocks.Most of the sites will be naturalised landscapes, with selected plots developed into pocket parks, gathering areas or places for urban agriculture. Cleveland Mayor Justin M. Bibb said, “This investment from the Bezos Earth Fund is a powerful endorsement of Cleveland’s commitment to neighborhood revitalization and environmental justice.”Indianapolis will restore land along the White RiverIn Indianapolis, the grant will support a 25-acre park at Reverend Mozel Sanders Park, along the White River. The project is intended to serve around 6,500 neighbourhood residents while also providing a destination for people elsewhere on the city's west side.Plans include wetland restoration, additional trees and expanded trails, together with basketball courts, multi-use sports fields, a community farm, an orchard and open lawns for gatherings. Two miles of new trails are expected to connect the park with existing regional greenways, giving pedestrians and cyclists more continuous routes through the area. Public art will also form part of the development, reflecting the history of the surrounding community.Jeff Bezos’ funding will bring trees and shade to Salt Lake CitySalt Lake City has selected two locations for its share of the funding: the 9-Line trail and Fleet Block. Both already have some of the infrastructure needed for public use, but lack the planted landscapes that would provide shade and make the areas greener.Along the 9-Line, the project will replace 3.2 acres of underused gravel with trees, water-efficient gardens and shaded areas. The work will extend along 1.7 miles of trail, which is used by more than 500,000 cyclists and pedestrians each year.The second site, Fleet Block, covers 2.4 acres in central Salt Lake City. The former industrial brownfield is due to become a public green space with a denser canopy of trees and other vegetation. Its location in the downtown area makes it a different kind of project from the trail improvements, bringing planted space to a site previously associated with industrial use.Mayor Erin Mendenhall described, “As our summers get hotter, shade and green space are no longer just nice additions—they are essential public infrastructure.”“I’m grateful the Bezos Earth Fund shares our vision on these projects, which will help us bring much-needed trees, water-wise landscaping, and new amenities to our city, creating a cooler, healthier, and more welcoming public spaces for the more than 16,000 Salt Lakers who live within a 10-minute walk.”Los Angeles will expand the green space around Watts TowersIn Los Angeles, the funding will help develop a five-acre park on the Watts Towers Arts Center campus. The site is an established cultural destination, but parts of its grounds remain underused. The proposed work will create more room for visitors to explore the campus and take part in arts and educational activities.The project is expected to improve the campus as a public gathering place while retaining its cultural purpose. The announcement estimates that the site attracts more than 50,000 visitors annually, and the expanded green space is intended to support its role as a community destination ahead of the 2028 Olympic Games.The Los Angeles Neighborhood Land Trust has worked with the Watts Towers Arts Center on community engagement, fundraising and design over the past 15 years. The new funding will help move that work towards construction, under the stewardship of the city.Little Rock will turn a former motorway ramp into a parkLittle Rock's 30 Crossing project will reclaim a 20-acre site in the city centre that became available following the removal of a cloverleaf exit ramp. The space is planned as a new destination park, connecting existing areas of public green space along the riverfront.The proposed park will link more than 100 acres of interconnected green space, including Riverfront Park and the grounds around the Clinton Presidential Center. The Bezos Earth Fund grant will support the initial phase of the project. According to the announcement, that contribution is intended to help attract a further $60 million to $70 million in fundraising for the development.Allentown and Atlanta will create parks for local residentsIn Allentown, Pennsylvania, the funding will be used to redevelop a 1.1-acre plot covered largely by asphalt in a neighbourhood particularly vulnerable to heat. The planned Franklin Park is expected to serve more than 16,000 residents.The design includes shade structures and trees, play areas for children and young people, accessible paths, seating and game tables. A community garden with water access and a basketball court will provide additional activities, while restrooms and parking are also included in the plans. Atlanta's Four Corners Park will cover 4.8 acres in Peoplestown, a neighbourhood in the city's southwest. The development, led by Park Pride, will provide accessible play and recreation areas, flexible gathering spaces and community gardening facilities, with composting and environmental infrastructure included in the design. The project has been shaped by residents' input and is expected to serve more than 3,500 people.Sioux Falls will reclaim a former quarryAt Falls Park in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, the project will transform a degraded industrial quarry into a 16.3-acre public park. The site sits beside one of the city's most diverse neighbourhoods and is expected to become a place where residents can spend time outdoors without leaving the area.The plans include trails, access to the water's edge and open spaces for gathering. Rather than filling the site with recreational facilities alone, the design will make use of the landscape itself, allowing visitors to explore the area and spend time near the water.The city's Parks and Recreation Department has committed to the long-term operation and maintenance of the park. That commitment is part of the wider approach, which requires cities to consider how the new spaces will be looked after once construction is complete.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Open de Espana: Grant Forrest continues good record to take one-stroke lead into the weekend in Madrid
articles.summary: Scotland's Grant Forrest nudged ahead of the pack to lead the Open de Espana after two rounds; compatriot Connor Syme shares second place with Switzerland's Joel Girrbach in Madrid; Spain's Eugenio Chacarra and Joe Dean of England are a shot further back
articles.body:
Forrest, who was at five-under-par alongside fellow Scotsman Conner Syme and Spain's Eugenio Chacarra at the end of Thursday's play, carded a four-under second-round 67 to move to nine under and open a one-stroke lead at Club de Campo Villa de Madrid.

Syme shot a second-round 68 and sits in joint-second place with Switzerland's Joel Girrbach, who rolled in five consecutive birdies from the fourth hole on the way to his 66.

"It was a really good score in the end," said Forrest, who has twice finished tied third in Spain's national open, in 2021 and 2024, and has never missed the cut across his six previous appearances.

"I didn't have my best stuff on our first five or six holes, but made a couple of really nice par saves to keep the momentum going, and then I just managed to make quite a few birdies.

"Started driving it well the last 12 holes and delighted with four under. I probably didn't play quite as well as yesterday.

"Obviously, I had a couple of good scores there [over past two days].

"It's hard to know when a day like Thursday will come when you shoot five under for nine holes and you fly up the board, or today was a bit more plodding along and then a couple came towards the end. I'm just going to keep the foot down."

Eugenio Chacarra, who is playing on home soil with a fractured toe, and England's Joe Dean are both at eight under, with Danish duo Jacob Skov Olesen and Jeff Winther a shot further back, alongside French pair Martin Couvra and Victor Perez and New Zealand's Daniel Hillier.

Patrick Reed, who has led the Race to Dubai Rankings since February, missed the cut and Chacarra would leapfrog both Rory McIlroy and the American with a victory on Sunday.

articles.title: Bears Announce Surprising Caleb Williams Decision Ahead of Packers Game
articles.summary: The Chicago Bears announce a surprising decision involving quarterback Caleb Williams ahead of Sunday's showdown with the Green Bay Packers. The post Bears A...
articles.body:
Caleb Williams carries a questionable tag into Sunday's game at Green Bay after returning to Chicago Bears practice Friday on a limited basis, according to the Friday injury report published by the Bears communications department.

Coach Ben Johnson named Tyson Bagent the starter Monday, yet Williams' Friday progress leaves open whether the Bears have another surprise planned after last week's one-snap start for Case Keenum.

Williams went through a limited session Friday, his first team practice since he hurt his hamstring Sept. 20 against the Minnesota Vikings, according to Shaw Local reporter Michal Dwojak. He took no first-team snaps, and the Bears listed him as questionable for the trip to Lambeau Field after two straight "out" designations.

"He's right on track," Johnson said Friday at Halas Hall, Dwojak reported. The coach added that Williams threw "a little bit" earlier in the week, that a progression is in place and that the return date remains "to be determined."

Johnson described a steady increase in running and throwing, with a throwing protocol every couple of days to check for setbacks. "So far, so good," he said. Dwojak noted the Bears will likely handle the return conservatively so the hamstring does not become a recurring problem.

The injury happened in the Week 2 loss to Minnesota. Williams strained the hamstring on a run without contact, needed help from the medical staff and was carted off, according to CBS Sports reporter Zachary Pereles .

ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported a Grade 2 strain with a typical recovery of three to four weeks, according to NBC Chicago .

NBC Chicago pointed to Sunday's game at Green Bay and the Oct. 18 game at Atlanta as the likely return dates if Williams missed multiple games. He already sat out the Sept. 28 game against the Philadelphia Eagles and the Oct. 4 game against the New York Jets . Those absences were the first of his career since Chicago made him the No. 1 overall pick in 2024.

Johnson set the tone shortly after the injury. Williams gets back "a lot faster than what people can anticipate," the coach said, according to the Chicago Sun-Times ' Jason Lieser and Patrick Finley .

Johnson declined to put a timeline on the recovery and called Williams week to week.

Bears Starter Decision After Case Keenum Twist

Johnson announced Monday on ESPN Chicago that Bagent "will be the guy" against Green Bay, according to CBS Sports . Bagent's start follows a 23-12 win over the Jets in which he completed 25 of 34 passes for 268 yards.

Dwojak's Friday report treated that announcement as standing and described Williams' chances of playing Sunday as unclear, since he got no first-team repetitions this week.

Johnson has already played a bluff this season. Keenum took the first snap against the Jets with Bagent lined up at wide receiver, then left the game, according to Pro Football Talk . Bagent handled every other snap, all 93 of them.

"Good for him," Johnson said when told the win would go on Keenum's record. The Elias Sports Bureau credited Keenum with the start and the victory because he took the first snap, PFT reported. Keenum is 2-0 as a starter for Chicago this season, while Bagent is 2-2 in his career.

Johnson has not set a return date for Williams. The Bears face the Packers at Lambeau Field on Sunday, then visit the Falcons on Oct. 18 and play the New England Patriots on Thursday night, Oct. 22. Whether Williams dresses Sunday stays unanswered until the Bears finalize their inactives before kickoff.

articles.title: Dak Prescott’s Brutal Blunder Sends George Pickens and Jerry Jones Into Wild Fury
articles.summary: The Dallas Cowboys’ loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers’ came after the team fell short in its comeback attempt, with Jerry Jones and George Pickens showing the...
articles.body:
The Dallas Cowboys' loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' came after the team fell short in its comeback attempt, with Jerry Jones and George Pickens showing their frustration afterward.

A late interception ended Dallas' final possession and sealed a 24-16 home defeat.

Cowboys owner Jerry Jones and WR react after Dallas' defeat

The Dallas Cowboys lost 24-16 to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at AT&T Stadium, with owner Jerry Jones and wide receiver George Pickens reacting after the game.

Before the game, the Buccaneers had an 0-4 record, while the Cowboys entered at 2-2. Despite the result, Pickens finished with nine receptions for 130 yards and one touchdown.

In the fourth quarter, Pickens caught a 17-yard touchdown pass that cut Dallas' deficit to 24-16. However, the Cowboys failed to convert the ensuing two-point attempt, leaving them needing another touchdown to get back into the game.

The Cowboys later regained possession and moved the ball to Tampa Bay's 24-yard line, giving the team an opportunity to score late in the fourth quarter. Dak Prescott threw toward tight end Jake Ferguson, but the pass hit Ferguson's hands and popped into the air. Buccaneers linebacker Alex Anzalone intercepted the deflected pass, giving the Buccaneers possession late in the fourth quarter.

After the interception, Jones was seen striking a table inside his suite, while Pickens threw his helmet on the sideline. BrickCenter_ shared a video of their reactions with the caption , "George Pickens and Jerry Jones are PISSED

Prescott's comments came after the Cowboys were unable to complete their comeback against the Bucs. The turnover ended the Cowboys' last possession of the game.

Cowboys fail to complete comeback against Buccaneers

Despite injury concerns, Dak Prescott started against the Buccaneers , completing 24 of 42 passes for 316 yards and one touchdown with two interceptions. The Dallas Cowboys committed three turnovers in the game. They finished with 366 total yards, compared with 419 for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, who held possession for 39 minutes and 21 seconds.

After the game, Prescott said , "We were definitely supposed to win this game." His comment reflected the team's disappointment after failing to get the result it expected.

CeeDee Lamb caught two passes for nine yards before leaving the game with a quadriceps injury. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers finished with 241 rushing yards in the game.

Bucky Irving carried the ball 21 times for 165 rushing yards and one rushing touchdown. He also scored a receiving touchdown and recorded a 72-yard run. Buccaneers quarterback Jalon Daniels completed 19 of 25 passes for 189 yards, one touchdown and one interception.

The loss leaves Dallas with a 2–3 record. The Cowboys will now turn their attention to their next game against the Green Bay Packers after falling short against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Airlines sound alarm on costs crisis' and 'King's £1.5m bailout'
articles.summary: The weekend edition of the Financial Times highlights what it is calling a "mounting crisis" for airlines.
articles.body:
The Guardian says for a party that began the year promising to turn voters' hunger for change into a serious challenge to Labour, the Green Party's defeat in the Holborn and St Pancras by election was a sobering moment. The Times suggests that " the Green Party's flirtation with extremism will inevitably backfire ."

Writing in the Daily Mail, Dan Hodges describes the result as "the most important rejection of anti-semitism since Cable Street" - and believes the Greens' humiliation could lead to an early election . But the Daily Mirror says Labour delivered a message of hope and inclusion.

The Daily Telegraph says the chairman of John Lewis and Waitrose has warned the Chancellor that if he imposes what's been described as a "warehouse tax" on retailers in the budget, it could be the final nail in the coffin for the high street.

The Daily Mail has a similar warning from the head of Marks and Spencer , who's urged John Healey to reverse what he calls the "mistakes of the last two budgets" to get Britain growing again.

The Times says Andy Burnham and the Chancellor have rejected a plea from the Health Secretary for more money for NHS pay in the budget. The paper says that in a highly unusual move, they have jointly written to Yvette Cooper to say that increases will have to be met from the existing budget.

The Daily Express says William and Catherine became the "Prince and Princess of sales" as they served customers during a visit to Ikea in Belfast. "Checkout who's behind the tills," is its headline.

The Sun leads with the story of the King, loaning his brother Andrew £1.5m for the repair bill at his former home, Royal Lodge. It's "a princely sum" suggests the Daily Mirror. " The king and I.O.U", is The Sun's headline .

images.caption: The weekend edition of the Financial Times highlights what it is calling a "mounting crisis" for airlines. It reports that persistently high fuel prices are forcing carriers to cut flights, axe costs and delay payments on leased aircraft. Noting the collapse of both Spirit Airlines and airBaltic earlier in the year, the paper has spoken to industry leaders, analysts and financiers, who said the "spectre of airlines falling over the winter season" was higher than it had been in previous years.

articles.title: Climbing Everest is hard. Recovering a body from near its summit will be even harder
articles.summary: The lime-green boots shine vividly against the dazzling white snow. A man in a knitted fleece smiles as he carefully attaches crampons in preparation for his historic ascent of the world’s tallest mountain.
articles.body: The lime-green boots shine vividly against the dazzling white snow. A man in a knitted fleece smiles as he carefully attaches crampons in preparation for his historic ascent of the world’s tallest mountain. The grainy, 30-year-old video is the last known footage of a climber whose identity has remained a mystery to all but a small circle of mountaineers since he died in a ferocious storm near the top of Mount Everest in 1996. The storm claimed eight lives and inspired Jon Krakauer’s best-selling first-hand account “Into Thin Air.” But the deaths and incredible stories of survival on the Nepal side of Everest have overshadowed one of the enduring mysteries of that day — the fate of three Indian climbers trying to summit the mountain via the more challenging approach from Tibet. For decades, the frozen body of one of those men has lain exposed, curled up as if asleep, at the spot where he died around 300 meters below the summit. For generations of climbers he has been known simply as “Green Boots” — due to those green Koflach shoes that protrude from the ice. But last year, in a covert, high-altitude operation, a small team of Sherpas successfully retrieved DNA samples from his corpse and gave him back his name. “Green Boots” is Dorje Morup, a mountaineer who grew up in northern India, near the border with Tibet, and served in a specialized Indian border police force. He was 47 when he died. Now that India has confirmed who he is, the race is on to bring Morup home. This year India’s government began searching for an elite team of Sherpas to embark on a risky mission: to bring back his body from the mountain’s death zone, where there is so little oxygen that humans cannot breathe unaided for long. “People knew ‘Green Boots’ as a landmark, but they didn’t know the person behind that title,” said Dawa Steven Sherpa, Nepali mountaineer and CEO of expedition company Asian Trekking. Footage obtained exclusively by CNN and testimony from those who were on the mountain paint a more detailed picture than before of Morup, the man who died serving his country and is now the goal of one of mountaineering’s grimmest challenges. It may be mission impossible. Several diplomatic hurdles will need to be surmounted before any recovery effort can take its first steps. And scaling Everest to above 8,000 meters and bringing down a body that has been frozen in ice for three decades will push any team to its limit. The mission also raises another difficult question: do you risk more lives to bring home a dead body? ‘Class-one mountaineers’ Heavy breaths are interspersed by the sound of crunching snow, as shaky, never-before-seen video pans to a team of climbers, several wearing green boots, traversing a white-snow field. Ahead, black dots move in formation like ants as Everest’s imposing upper flanks loom above them. It’s spring 1996 and the climbers are hoping to become the first Indian team to summit Everest from its more challenging northern route. Their day jobs are with the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), a specialized force tasked with guarding the peaks and passes of India’s 2,167-mile (3,488-kilometer) long Himalayan border with China. Formed in the aftermath of a disastrous mountain war with China in 1962, the ITBP operates in some of the most inhospitable terrain on Earth. It recruits prominently from communities living in India’s high Himalaya mountains. Alongside Morup were two other Indian climbers who hailed from Ladakh, a remote mountainous territory bordering Tibet: Tsewang Paljor and Tsewang Smanla. The three were “class-one mountaineers” who were close “like family,” according to one of their fellow climbers. The never-before-seen expedition footage captures the camaraderie and humor among the team. Inside a tent, one man serves food from a steaming saucepan. He’s one of the team leaders, and as he hands out the plates the rest of the team joke about the inversion of hierarchy. In another scene, a group of climbers are chatting together next to a cluster of tents. “When I get up there, I’m going to do this,” one man says, making a drinking gesture. But getting up there would prove deadly. The last person to see them alive Hundreds of miles from the snow and ice of the Himalaya, a modest house in the plains of India’s Punjab state holds memories of the last hours of Morup’s life. It’s the home of veteran mountaineer Harbhajan Singh, a leader on the ill-fated expedition, and one of the last people to see Morup, Paljor and Smanla alive. Old furniture fills the rooms, giving the place the domestic, lived-in feel of a family home that has grown with its occupants. However, the medals, photographs and awards hung in the hall tell an extraordinary story of a life spent never far from danger in the mountains. Now 70, the retired ITBP inspector general points out Morup, Paljor and Smanla in video shared with CNN during a visit to his home and smiles as he flips through photo albums. He had climbed before with them in the Indian Himalaya and was amazed by their strength. “I have not seen them tired,” he said. As the team collapsed into their tents at the end of each grueling day on Everest, it was invariably Morup, Paljor and Smanla who still had the energy to brew tea and revive spirits, he remembered. Morup was easygoing and a “silent worker,” said Singh. “Whenever we were given any task, like fixing the ropes, he would always volunteer. He was technically very sound, physically very sound.” The first time the team saw Everest was awe-inspiring, Singh said. “I bowed my head out of respect,” he added. “It was very beautiful.” But the team was not there to admire the scenery. There was a job to be done, and national prestige at stake. A successful Indian ascent of Everest from the north side “was a matter of pride,” he said. Several other teams were on the mountain, including from Japan, Norway, and a British team making a documentary with actor Brian Blessed. “It was wonderful,” Singh said. “Everyone was excited.” The summit push After weeks of arduous climbing, Singh led a six-man team, including Morup, Paljor and Smanla above the final camp located at 8,300 meters (27,000 feet). They were just over 500 meters from the summit. Their task on May 10, Singh said, was to open up a route to the Second Step and test the stability of a ladder fixed to the rock face. The step is an almost vertical 40-meter bottleneck, and the most technically challenging part of the climb. Beyond was the last stretch to the summit, typically about a four-hour climb in normal conditions. If the weather was good, they could make a summit attempt, Singh said. But it was late in the day and despite favorable weather reports, Singh said he could see clouds forming above Everest: An omen that bad weather was on its way. He decided not to proceed. “If you try you will not be able to come back,” Singh had told Morup, Paljor and Smanla. But the three decided to push on and later phoned base camp to say they were making an attempt for the summit. “I was the last one (to see them alive),” Singh said. “They had a cup of tea at the Second Step… As they were going up, I saw them fixing the rope. I thought, ok they will come back,” he added. At such heights with so little oxygen, “you cannot judge whether you will be trapped,” Singh said. “You have only one aim: I have to climb Everest.” Singh and another climber turned back for the high camp. By the time they reached the safety of the tents at 6 p.m., Morup, Paljor and Smanla had radioed base camp. They had summited. “All of us were very happy,” said Singh. “But it was very short-lived.” A deadly storm The storm quickly rolled in, catching many climbers on both sides of the mountain off guard. On the Nepal side, American mountaineers Scott Fischer and Doug Hansen died, as well as New Zealand’s Rob Hall and Andy Harris, and Japan’s Yasuko Namba. Down at Advanced Base Camp on the Tibetan side, the anxious Indian team could see two headlamps light up their descent high on the mountain. “One of the beams spiraling downwards, toward the Second Step. Then darkness, as they went out of our lives,” the expedition’s senior deputy leader PM Das said in a written account. The Second Step would have been “very challenging” to descend in those conditions, said Jon Gangdal, a Norwegian climber leading a separate expedition on the north side of Everest and who was in contact with the Indian team. “What hits the mountain so high are these jet stream winds,” he told CNN. Those winds are full of snow and ice, and bring gusts of 150-200 kilometers per hour, plunging temperatures to minus 60 to 80 degrees Celsius (minus 79 to minus 112 Fahrenheit). “And the higher you are, the stronger the winds are,” Gangdal said. Exposure, coupled with a lack of oxygen, rapidly becomes an “extremely dangerous” situation, he added. Before the summit attempt, Gangdal described a feeling of “competition” between the Indian and Japanese teams to be the first to summit that season. Summit fever – an irrational drive to reach to the top, whatever it takes – may have taken over the climbers, he believes. At base camp, “everybody is only heading for one thing, summit, summit, summit,” said Gangdal, author of “Guilt and Glory: Climbing with Sherpas.” “As soon as you are on the ridge… you get the feeling that (the summit) is within reach.” A few days later a second team from the Indian expedition summited Everest. For Gangdal, who helped try and rouse the team leaders into mounting a rescue, that was the wrong move. “They should have put in effort to get the bodies down first,” he said. Paljor is believed to have fallen off the mountain; his body was never found. Smanla lay above the Second Step before he too disappeared. And Morup, who managed to descend in the storm, lay near the trail below the First Step in a small limestone cave, his Green Boots visible in the snow. American climber David Roeske, who summited Everest in 2013 and 2016, said passing Morup was an “opportunity to pay homage” and “felt like you were honoring him and his memory best by pausing there and taking note.” “It was a beautiful opportunity to remember this man’s experience and life and to move gently and humbly up the mountain yourself… his memory lived on in a very powerful way by being there for so long,” he said. ‘We always knew’ The upper reaches of Everest are home to many of the more than 300 climbers who have perished on the mountain. Rescues this high are risky and expensive, and helicopters cannot safely fly at such altitudes. Among them was US climber Francys Arsentiev, who died in 1998 after becoming the first American woman to summit without supplemental oxygen. Her body remained visible for a decade before it was removed from view, and she became known as “Sleeping Beauty” for the peaceful way she rested on the mountain. Previous attempts to retrieve bodies at such high altitudes have been called off because of the risk of death to the rescuers. The document issued by the ITBP inviting bids to retrieve Morup’s body does not say why it is trying to do so now, 30 years after his death – although some of the members of the 1996 Indian expedition have since attained high rank in the organization. “We felt that any brave ITBP mountaineer should be given a dignified farewell,” an ITBP official told CNN in response to queries on the timing of the proposed expedition. “Someone who made the supreme sacrifice in the line of duty at high altitude should be given that dignity.” The ITBP official said they identified Morup after carrying out “a detailed examination of the available expedition records, took inputs from surviving expedition members and considered the technical inputs.” But those in the industry “have always known” Green Boots was Morup, said Dawa Steven Sherpa, whose mountaineering company Asian Trekking outfitted the 1996 Indian expedition. Proving it was a complex operation. Dawa said his company “without very much fanfare, without making it too public” launched “a very small expedition to send a group of Sherpas up,” to extract DNA samples from the frozen corpse’s hair and nails. The team was relying on bottled oxygen so “we needed to act quickly to get whatever DNA samples we could,” Dawa said. “You do not want to be spending too long doing this, and finishing off your oxygen, or putting yourself in a position where you wasted so much time that you could get the team in trouble.” Under that time pressure, the team had to carefully handle the precious DNA to prevent the risk of contamination on their descent. A lab in India later confirmed the samples belonged to Morup. Bringing Dorje home Though there will be challenges, bringing Morup off the mountain is possible, said Dawa. His body has been frozen solid for 30 years, making him much heavier to move. But a team of about eight Sherpas could do it – using foam padding and a special stretcher that cocoons the body, Dawa said. “You’re able to then bring the body down by dragging it, and it will slide over rocks and ice,” he said. “You need a couple of extra hands just to make sure that the body doesn’t slide off down the mountain.” Complicating the retrieval is the position of Morup’s body, and the risk that it could be damaged or start decomposing on the way down. “If (limbs are) outstretched, there’s no way to push it back in… It’s frozen solid, so it really does make that really, really hard,” he said. “You could break the limb, if it catches on a rock and then gets twisted.” Cultural sensitivities around Sherpas handling a dead body would also need to be respected, said Dawa. “It’s not just any dead body… this is a Ladakhi climber who is very similar in terms of culture and religion in ways that a Sherpa can see himself in that,” he added. The ITBP official said the mission is now expected to happen during the April-May climbing season of 2027 after “taking everything into account — necessary approvals, clearances and everything else.” It is unclear whether any companies will make a bid for next year. Any mission will also need diplomatic buy-in from China, which closed the Tibetan side of Everest to foreign climbers this year. Ties between the two countries remain strained over their long-running Himalayan border dispute, which erupted into a deadly skirmishes in 2020 that saw soldiers from both sides use rocks and iron rods in brutal hand-to-hand combat. CNN has reached out to the Chinese Mountaineering Association and the Sports Bureau of Tibet Autonomous Region for comment on the proposed mission to retrieve Morup’s body. Repeated calls to the China Tibet Mountaineering Association, which manages permits for Everest’s north route, went unanswered. “It should have happened 30 years ago,” Gangdal said. “This is the Indian responsibility to bring this guy down, especially when they learnt that he became like a death marker on the mountain.” Singh and Dawa say it would be an important achievement if Morup is finally brought home to his family. “There is closure for families when you bring a body down, when you give it a proper burial,” said Dawa. “In another way, you are humanizing the person again.”

articles.title: MPs criticise Green Hill Solar Farm approval in Northamptonshire
articles.summary: Conservative MPs Stuart Andrew and Sarah Bool oppose the construction of Green Hill Solar Farm.
articles.body:
Two Conservative MPs have criticised the approval of plans for one of the biggest solar farms in the country.

Stuart Andrew, the MP for Daventry and Sarah Bool, the MP for South Northamptonshire, claimed Green Hill Solar Farm would take up farmland and change the countryside.

The development, which was approved on Thursday, will go ahead across about 2,965 acres (1,200 hectares) of land south and west of Wellingborough, north of Northampton and parts of Buckinghamshire.

When speaking to Annabel Amos on BBC Northampton, Andrew said: "We're going to see villages in my constituency being surrounded by these huge solar farms and it will change the landscape and... we will lose good arable land."

Bool said in a statement she was "incredibly disappointed" and was "taking stock" of the decision to make "versatile land" not available to arable farming.

The size of the project meant that recommendations for the scheme were made by the Planning Inspectorate, rather than local planning authorities.

The inspectorate's examination stage took more than five months to complete, opening in October 2025 and closing in April.

More than 1,200 people and businesses sent comments about the plans.

Juliet Jarvis, from the Stop Green Hill Solar campaign group, said she was "pretty devastated" by the news.

She said the panels, which she compared in size to "double decker buses", would surround Grendon and Easton Maudit and cause "disruption during construction".

"Once the solar farm is in place, it will completely change the face of Northamptonshire countryside.

"We would like to see... appropriate brownfield sites covered with solar panels before we take up our best and most versatile agricultural land and risk destroying rural communities which is what we fear will happen here," Jarvis added.

Labour peer Baroness Curran, the parliamentary under-secretary of state in the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, said: "Solar power is crucial to delivering energy security for the country and financial security for communities, families and businesses.

"By securing more homegrown power we control, we are driving a generational opportunity to grow our economy and tackle the root cause of sky-high energy bills: our exposure to volatile global fossil fuel markets."

Island Green Power, the company behind the scheme, "welcomed" the government's decision.

Chief executive Bob Psaradellis said: "This decision again confirms that Island Green Power produces high-quality nationally significant infrastructure proposals that will benefit Britain.

"The benefits will be shared with communities, through a local benefit fund, and the wider country, through the increase in secure, clean and cheap homegrown power."

Renewable energy expert Rhiannon De Wreede said she "sympathised" with campaigners but added that large solar farms were "needed" alongside more rooftop panels.

Green Hill Solar said the farm would "benefit Britain with clean, secure, low-cost energy".

It said the scheme could generate 500 megawatts of electricity to power about 200,000 homes.

It is hoped construction will begin in 2027, with the aim of providing electricity to homes by 2029, the company said.

articles.title: Zerodha’s Dinesh Pai sees an upside in US green card suspension for TCS, Infosys, Wipro: If US companies can’t bring talent to the US, they probably will...
articles.summary: The US decision to suspend eight technology and IT services companies, including TCS, Infosys, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from its green card labour
articles.body: The US decision to suspend eight technology and IT services companies, including TCS, Infosys, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from its green card labour certification programme has left many Indian professionals in America worried about their long-term plans. Zerodha’s Dinesh Pai, however, sees an upside for India. In a post on X, Pai said that if US companies cannot bring talent to the US, they will probably bring the work to India instead.The suspension was announced on October 8 by US Vice President JD Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling. Alongside the four Indian IT majors, the list names Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant and Capgemini. The US Department of Labor will neither accept new nor process pending applications from these companies under the Permanent Labor Certification programme, known as PERM. It is the step an employer must clear before sponsoring a foreign worker for an employment-based green card. US officials cited alleged fraud and the displacement of American workers.Fewer Indians in the US could mean lower remittancesPai began with the downside. India receives about $125 billion in remittances a year, the most of any country, and the US accounts for roughly a quarter of it, over $30 billion. Fewer high-earning Indians settling in the US could eventually shrink that flow.He added that fewer Indians in top American jobs could also mean less soft power for the country and less angel capital coming into Indian startups.GCCs and AI startups in India could gain from the green card freezeThe upside, in Pai’s view, lies in Global Capability Centres (GCCs). He expects them to expand further in India, which already hosts more than 2,100 GCCs employing about 2.4 million people. He also sees more top engineering talent staying back to build Indian companies and AI startups, rather than working under visa uncertainty abroad. Pai ended his post by asking followers what else he was missing.Microsoft and TCS have both defended their records. Microsoft said 80% of its roughly 6,000 H-1B applications in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees. TCS said it does not expect a material impact on its workforce strategy, as its PERM filings were in single digits over the past two years. It still plans to hire 15,000 more people in the US over the next five years.For employees, the suspension does not cancel existing H-1B visas or green cards already granted. It halts the PERM route through these eight employers, and no end date has been announced. That means a longer wait for those already in the queue, and possibly more reason for some of that talent and work to stay in India, as Pai suggests.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Green Party MP wants to make sure it is 'not vulnerable to extremists'
articles.summary: The party's Westminster leader Ellie Chowns made the comments after ex-leader Caroline Lucas said some members had joined to vote in the Zionism motion.
articles.body:
A Green Party MP has said her party needs to make sure it is not "vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists" after members voted for a motion that claimed Zionism was racism.

The motion put forward by activists, which became formal policy after it was approved at the Green's conference earlier this month, has divided senior party figures and been criticised by Jewish groups.

Westminster leader Ellie Chowns told the BBC it was a "significant and damaging policy" and she would work to reform the Green Party.

It comes after ex-leader Caroline Lucas said it was not being protected from entryism - where people sign up to a party to try to change it.

The controversial policy also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme on Saturday, Chowns said: "I don't know if there are extremists and racists in my party. But I want to make sure that my party isn't vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists."

The MP described Zionism as a "contested concept" and said the motion did not represent the views of the large majority of Green Party members, "nor of people in the country".

Chowns said the motion would be a "distraction from the very important work" the party has been doing campaigning for Palestinian rights.

She added: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813.

There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.

The motion, among other statements, "supports the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants".

It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said: "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it."

Appearing on BBC Radio 4 programme Any Questions on Friday, Lucas said she was not putting any blame on the party's current leader, Zack Polanski, who she said had done "great things" for the party.

"Our constitution was written decades ago, well before we had MPs, before we had mayors, before we had anything like the number of that we have today," the ex-leader said.

Lucas, who was for years the face of the Greens as its first and sole MP until 2024, added the party needed to be made "a welcoming place for Jewish people."

A Green Party spokesperson said: "Green Party membership has increased since Zack Polanksi announced his leadership bid in May 2025. Unlike other political parties, our members can bring and set policy.

"This is one motion alongside dozens of others that was discussed at our biggest-ever party conference. Every motion submitted to conference undergoes debate and no single interest group drives policy. "

Polanski, who is Jewish, previously told the BBC he would not have voted for the motion and instead would have voted for an amended version.

However, he said the "substantial part of the motion", that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology" was "obvious".

Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

Ashok Kumar, a Green Party member and part of the Greens for Palestine group, voted for the motion and told the BBC last week it was about "Palestinian liberation."

He said he didn't feel the vote was harming the image of the Green Party, and that a growing number of people see this as a core issue.

"They see the violence that's (been) occurring over the last three years," he told BBC Politics Live. "So, I think the Zionist position is actually the marginal position.

Following Polanksi's by-election defeat in Holborn and St Pancras this week, the leader of the Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein said he should resign.

She added it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.

Polanski did not stay at conference to vote on the motion or amendments. He left early to campaign for the north London by-election, which Labour won on Thursday with Greens coming second.

Following his defeat, Polanski told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and he "of course" had not questioned that.

He lost out to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali - who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22 percentage points on the 2024 general election.

articles.title: The Future, Sadly, Is Now in Soylent Green, the Classic Sci-Fi Film That Just Got an Arrow Video Release
articles.summary: Soylent Green Blu-ray review: The future, sadly, is now.
articles.body:
It’s the United States of the 2020s. Climate change has created a perpetual heat wave, pollution has contaminated the air, and overpopulation combined with the consolidation of wealth and power in the hands of a select and self-interested few has resulted in major cities becoming seas of human bodies with no space and barely any resources to live. The elite can still access clean water and fresh food, but they live under guard in isolated palatial homes with women who are deprived of autonomy. The rest eat food increasingly processed and surely riddled with pathogens, and intellect and education has been eradicated for the masses, with only the elderly recalling the value of reading and academia.

So I thought: Why not watch an old favorite film instead of focusing on the real world like this? Thanks to Arrow Video, I can, through this new 4K UHD and Blu-ray release. “What is the secret of Soylent Green?” is the question asked of everyone that saw the trailer for this Charlton Heston-starring dystopian sci-fi classic way back in 1973 (concluding an apocalyptic “trilogy” for Heston that began with 1968’s Planet of the Apes and 1971’s The Omega Man ). But can anyone in 2026 come to this film not knowing the crucial revelation upon which the entire plot relies? Maybe, since we’re now in such a fragmented era of media consumption, with people far less likely to watch the same things, not to mention that there’s even more of a tendency to ignore the old in favor of the new. If fresh eyes do fall on Soylent Green , they may just be surprised, and I don’t want to do anything to rob them of that experience. So believe it or not, no spoilers here; it may be a futile effort, but if anyone makes any obvious jokes or references in the comments below, at least it won’t be me.

Charlton Heston called Soylent Green “the best B movie ever made,” but it’s so much more. At its most fundamental, the film is a noirish police procedural with a hard-bitten detective, a damsel in distress, and a global conspiracy that’s bigger than both of them. A board member of the Soylent corporation — supplier of processed food wafers like the new Soylent Green, made from plankton — named Simonson (Joseph Cotten in a very brief appearance) has been brutally murdered, and Robert Thorn (Heston) is assigned to crack the case. Police work is completely corrupt, however, so Thorn spends more time lifting luxuries from Simonson’s opulent pad and availing himself of the “furniture,” otherwise known as Shirl (Leigh Taylor-Young) — one of the many women in this world whose life has been reduced to domestic imprisonment and sexual servitude in apartments occupied by their elite masters. With Simonson dead, Shirl will soon meet the new tenant that she’ll be required to serve; for now, at least, she has Thorn.

This is a relentlessly moist movie; to convey the oppressive levels of heat, the entire cast is drenched in stage sweat except when in the domains of the wealthy (and a certain elderly-centered facility late in the film). The movie is also largely drab and awash in beiges and grays, but the color palette pops when necessary with bright saturated colors that really shine on this new release, whether it’s a rare strawberry or a blue dress. It looks beautiful and rich, but with a grain that feels right for the period; I’m not sure if it was always there, but there’s an additional haze that looks particularly appropriate and oppressive whenever we’re outside in the heat, with a greenish tint that reminds us Soylent Green is omnipresent.

The movie is also a masterclass in world-building, beginning with a montage created by Charles Braverman (based on his 1968 short film, “American Time Capsule”). With bombastic music by Fred Myrow (whose scoring is kept minimal in the rest of the film), the rapid-fire depiction of the country’s industrial development and degradation sets the Soylent-laden stage. Opening scenes set in Thorn’s apartment juxtaposed with the home of the wealthy Simonson perfectly delineate the ways in which the two main tiers of society operate in this far-flung future of 2022, as well as the kinds of relationships that define their lives.

(And yes, Star Trek: Deep Space Nine drew on this concept for their two-part episode, “Past Tense,” and even referenced soylent in prop posters. And yes, the film’s co-star Brock Peters is Sisko’s dad on DS9. Moving on…)

Despite being part of a deeply damaged system, there’s a nobility to Heston’s Thorn and a dedication to the truth that drives him to actually do his job. Much of that comes from his long-term father-son relationship with his “book,” Solomon Roth (Edward G. Robinson), an elderly former college professor and live-in research assistant who provides Thorn with crucial investigative support. Their bond provides the emotional core of the movie, no doubt at least partially informed by their previous work together in The Ten Commandments (1956) and the original makeup tests for Planet of the Apes, where Robinson played Zaius (he dropped out of the actual film for health reasons). Thorn’s relationship with Chief Hatcher (Brock Peters) is another great touch. Hatcher relies on his colleague and friend to regularly fix his watch, and Thorn tinkers away, thus letting us know he’s rather smart for this world too… but only to a point. When he finally admits he can no longer repair the watch, it’s symbolic of something much larger; there are some things that will be beyond his ability to fix.

The film features a solid supporting cast that all add so much to even the smallest roles, including former Rifleman Chuck Connors as bodyguard Tab, the mesmerizing Paula Kelly as Tab’s girlfriend (roommate?) Martha, and the unctuous Leonard Stone as the apartment manager/pimp, Charles. In particular, fellow Omega Man alum Lincoln Kilpatrick turns up as Paul, a priest with knowledge that’s eating him away from within, and he even gets to reference the title of the 1966 Harry Harrison novel that serves as this film’s inspiration, Make Room! Make Room! Celia Lovsky (Vulcan matriarch T’Pau from the Star Trek original series episode “Amok Time”) also appears as the leader of the Exchange, where Sol and other “books” meet to share sources and information. She gets to tee up the obligatory “is Chuck actually God” joke, and when Sol brings her a rare volume never seen by the Exchange before, her trembling hands reaching reverently for the cover of the book is so evocative of everything that’s been lost.

But in many ways, this is Robinson’s film. A scene in which he eats real food with such relish and then realizes how profoundly sad it is that they’ve come to this state is a study in expertly modulated acting. The veteran actor knew he was dying even as he completed his last role — he passed away two months after finishing filming — and he brings every bit of experience and pain to a beautiful performance that also seems to push Heston to up his game. As a bookend to the film’s expertly-crafted opening, the film’s finale is a harrowing journey to the truth that begins when Sol makes a fateful decision that leads him and Thorn to the conclusion of the investigation and the movie’s big reveal. There’s a moment during that final sequence, when Thorn hears the secret of Soylent Green (but the audience doesn’t yet ) from Sol himself and is moved to tears; it will haunt you for days afterward.

While there is a new 2025 commentary track recorded for Arrow with film historian Michael Brooke and author Johnny Mains, there aren’t many other extras here you wouldn’t have encountered in previous releases of the film, including image galleries, the trailer, vintage featurettes about the making of the movie and its landmark position as Robinson’s 101st film, and an archival 2003 commentary track with director Richard Fleischer and actress Leigh Taylor-Young. Fleischer covers the thematic and production elements, while Taylor-Young chimes in to discuss her environmental work at the UN, her view of the film as a “harbinger,” and her attempt at a Ten Commandments joke during her shower scene with Heston. You can hear Heston briefly discuss the film during an audio-only 1985 BFI appearance, while Fleischer touches on it in a 1994 BFI interview captured on video that also covers his memories of the blacklisting era.

Perhaps most significant, however, in terms of additions for this new release is a booklet presenting material written by Dr. Alexandra Heller-Nicholas (who I recently encountered via her superb contributions to Severin Films’ Sangster Directs Hammer box set ). I’d like to tell you more about it, but I can’t , because Arrow didn’t provide an actual release copy for review. It was very nice to at least receive the screener disc, but as these reviews are about celebrating and supporting physical releases, that includes all aspects of the presentation. I have to assume Dr. Nichols’ work is exemplary as always; her attention to detail and respect for history is surely better than Arrow’s, which sent an accompanying press release listing other classic ’70s sci-fi films “Wetworld” and “The Andromeda Syndrome.” JFC, Arrow.

articles.title: Ludvig Aberg: “Si Rahm y Olazábal están en el vestuario de Europa en la Ryder, nuestro equipo es mejor”
articles.standfirst: El sueco de 26 años está llamado a competir por el número 1 mundial. "Será un largo camino", confiesa a MARCA, pero está en ello. Esta semana está jugando el Open de España
articles.summary: El sueco de 26 años está llamado a competir por el número 1 mundial. "Será un largo camino", confiesa a MARCA, pero está en ello. Esta semana está jugando el Open de España
articles.body: Ludvig Aberg (26 años, Eslov, Suecia) es uno de los mejores jugadores de golf del mundo. Como amateur fue junto a Jon Rahm el único golfista en la historia en ganar el prestigioso Ben Hogan Award -al mejor jugador universitario amateur de Estados Unidos- en dos ocasiones consecutivas. En 2022 rechazó un contrato de LIV Golf y su irrupción como profesional en 2023 fue fulgurante. El capitán de la Ryder Cup Luke Donald lo apremió a lograr resultados que justificaran su elección de cara a la cita de Roma y fue y ganó el European Masters. Demostró que era un fuera de serie. Ahora está en Madrid disputando el Open de España presented by Madrid y hasta ahora ha volado bajo el radar. Hoy ha destacado con una vuelta de 67 (208 total), pero tendrá complicada la victoria el domingo, como él mismo comenta a MARCA: “Creo que estoy un poco retrasado para ganar mañana; necesitaría algo de ayuda de los demás. Pero sí, creo que algunos aspectos de mi juego han sido buenos. He tenido algunas dificultades con los golpes de salida; obviamente, estas calles son bastante estrechas. Si pegas bien el drive, generas muchas oportunidades, pero siento que no he sabido aprovecharlas del todo. Hasta hoy no había jugado muy bien los pares 5, que son un factor clave aquí. Así que, si logras hacerlo bien... En fin, espero jugar bien mañana y escalar algunas posiciones en la clasificación”. El jugador sueco es una de las grandes novedades este año en el Abierto nacional, un torneo que ha elegido para completar su calendario: “Dada la forma en que funcionan las temporadas del PGA Tour y del DP World Tour, me encantaría jugar algunos torneos del DPWT en otoño. Obviamente, es muy difícil hacerlo cuando estás en plena temporada en Estados Unidos, pero esta época del año es un buen momento para ello. Jugué en Francia hace dos semanas y ahora estoy jugando este torneo; es mi primera vez aquí y la impresión que me he llevado hasta ahora ha sido muy buena”. Aberg, 18 clasificado del mundo, confirma lo positivo de su experiencia en el Open: “Todo el mundo se ha portado de maravilla. Jugué las dos primeras rondas con Ángel Ayora, y había muchos españoles siguiéndolo y apoyándolo; fue genial jugar en ese ambiente. El público ha estado fantástico durante toda la semana y el campo de golf supone, sin duda, un gran desafío”. En este sentido, aunque Aberg juega sobre todo en el PGA Tour, está encantado de conocer nuevos torneos e incluso recomienda las nuevas experiencias: “Bueno, solo puedo hablar por mí mismo; obviamente, en esta época del año paso mucho tiempo en Europa. Al ser de Suecia y vivir allí, resulta muy fácil venir aquí a jugar estos torneos, y hasta ahora han sido unas semanas estupendas. Sin duda, lo recomendaría”. Sobre Ayora, su compañero en esas dos primeras rondas, le preguntamos. “Es un gran jugador. Me impresionó la forma en que golpeaba la bola; su golpeo era realmente sólido. Obviamente todavía es muy joven, pero parece que está aprendiendo. Da la impresión de que tiene un amplio repertorio de golpes, especialmente en el juego corto. Será emocionante seguir su evolución a medida que mejore”, respondió. Con el malagueño compartió una concentración del equipo europeo la Ryder Cup. Hasta ahora su contacto con españoles en esta competición había sido con Rahm y Olazábal (vicecapitán). “Obviamente, Jon Rahm es una figura clave en esos torneos. Es un tipo imponente que transmite una gran imagen tanto en el vestuario como en la sala del equipo, al igual que José María. Obviamente, su experiencia, sus conocimientos y las historias que cuentan son fantásticos y a menudo resultan muy emotivos. Aportan muchísimo al equipo de la Ryder Cup, tanto en la sala del equipo como dentro y fuera del campo de golf; y si ellos dos están en la sala del equipo, el equipo es mejor”. Aberg, un tipo muy atlético de 1,90, nos habla también de su etapa como futbolista: “Obviamente elegí el deporte adecuado. Elegí el golf en lugar del fútbol, lo cual creo que fue un acierto, pero sigo viéndolo mucho. Soy muy aficionado del Liverpool, así que lo veo siempre que puedo; aunque, claro, no tenía el nivel suficiente para ser jugador”. ¿El Liverpool? Cuando era más joven, Steven Gerrard era mi gran ídolo. Era mi jugador favorito. Y cuando jugaba, quería ser como él. Y luego fichamos a Fernando Torres en 2007, o algo así”. Ludvig no es un jugador cualquiera. Es un golfista de clase mundial y este año ha firmado un gran papel en los cuatro Majors. Se ha alejado en el ranking de jugadores como Scheffler y McIlory, pero no tardará en regresar al ‘top 5’ mundial. “¿El número 1 del mundo? Obviamente Scottie Scheffler lleva una ventaja considerable respecto al segundo, pero siento que si sigo mejorando y progresando... Jugué con Scottie hace un par de semanas y hay muchas cosas que se pueden aprender de él; ojalá pueda aplicarlas a mi propio juego y algún día alcanzarlo, aunque supongo que será un camino largo”.

articles.title: Open de Espana: Joe Dean and Grant Forrest share one-shot lead going into final round in Madrid
articles.summary: Scotland's Grant Forrest and England's Joe Dean are the joint-leaders on 13-under par at the Real Club de Campo Villa de Madrid going into the final round; Watch the Open de Espana live on Sky Sports Golf from 12pm on Sunday
articles.body:
Forrest began the day with a one-shot advantage at the Real Club de Campo Villa de Madrid but slipped down the leaderboard after bogeying the fifth hole.

However, birdies at the 11th, 14th and 16th gave the Scot a four-under-par round of 67 and a total of 13 under.

Forrest, who is searching for his third DP World Tour title, said on europeantour.com : "I'm happy with how I handled today.

"I didn't have my best stuff but I'm really proud of how I dug in and made some nice putts, a couple of good recovery shots, and all in all a decent score again.

"This is one of my favourite tournaments, it's been good to me in the past, and I'd love nothing more than to go home with a trophy tomorrow."

His round was enough to leave him tied for the lead alongside Sheffield's Dean, who will feel he should have produced an even better outcome than the 65 he signed for.

Dean, a former delivery driver, who secured his maiden victory on the European-based circuit at the British Masters, followed five birdies on the front nine with three more at the 12th, 14th and 15th to open up a three-shot lead.

But the 32-year-old then double-bogeyed the 16th and dropped another shot at 17 before finishing on a high with a 31-foot putt for birdie on the last.

"It gave a little bit of hope after those previous two holes," said Dean. "We'll go again and see what happens."

France's Victor Perez and Dane Jacob Skov Olesen both also posted rounds of 65 to move to 12 under, one shot off the lead, alongside Joel Girrbach of Switzerland, who was round in 67.

Angel Ayora is the leading Spanish hope and he sits three shots off the lead after a 66 on a day of low scoring.

Shane Lowry produced his best round of the week with a four-under 67 boosting him into a tie for 17th but still trails by eight shots.

articles.title: US PERM suspension may boost India’s tech talent base, GCC expansion
articles.summary: US suspends PERM processing for 8 tech firms, potentially boosting India’s tech talent retention and accelerating GCC expansion and AI hiring demand.
articles.body: Hyderabad: The US govt’s suspension of PERM labour-certification processing for eight major technology companies is unlikely to disrupt the Indian IT sector immediately, but industry leaders say it could strengthen India’s ability to retain and attract high-end technology talent while accelerating the country’s global capability centre (GCC) expansion. PERM is a key stage in employer-sponsored green card applications that allows US companies to seek permanent residency for foreign workers.“US organizations will need to accelerate their GCC plans. Doing so will allow them to continue with their technology and engineering roadmap while reducing or maintaining their cost structure,” said former Goldman Sachs managing director and now co-founder of GCC Foundry Sandeep Dhar.However, HYSEA president Flt Lt Bipin Chandra Pendyala felt the move would not dramatically alter business models. “Companies such as Microsoft, Cognizant, TCS or Adobe already have a pretty large presence in the US and India. If they cannot do a certain number of green cards or H-1Bs next year because of this caveat, it is not that they will move all those roles to India. Pure development roles may move to India or other locations, but customer-facing, account management, customer success positions will need to remain in the US,” Pendyala said.Sidhant Rastogi, president of consulting and GCC enablement firm Zinnov, said some Indian professionals in the US may reassess their long-term plans, but any reversal of brain drain will depend on whether India offers comparable leadership roles, compensation and cutting-edge work. “What has fundamentally changed is the opportunity that India now offers,” Rastogi said, citing growth in AI, product engineering, platform development and global leadership roles.Neeti Sharma, CEO, TeamLease Digital, said the restrictions could benefit India’s tech and GCC ecosystem where 2,100 GCCs employ 2.4 million professionals, positioning the country for rising AI talent demand that is projected at 1.3 million by 2027. “More American companies may consider expanding their technology and AI operations here. articles.title: Pro Golfer’s Penalty Shows Rules Matter More Than Winning
articles.summary: Adam Hadwin took a two-stroke penalty for a wrong spot. This move proves integrity still counts on the Korn Ferry Tour.
articles.body:
Adam Hadwin faces a steep climb to regain his PGA Tour card after taking a two-stroke penalty for playing from the wrong spot. The 38-year-old Canadian self-reported the error on the par-3 second hole at the Korn Ferry Tour Championship. He needed to win the tournament to secure his playing rights for next season. This penalty changed his par to a double bogey and hurt his chances of a low score.

The rules official assessed the penalty because Hadwin took a full club-length of relief instead of the allowed scorecard length. Preferred lies were in effect at The Federal Club due to weather, according to Yahoo . He lifted and cleaned his ball but moved it too far. He saw his playing partners take the shorter relief and then notified the rules official. This honesty cost him strokes but saved his reputation.

A new local rule took effect at the start of 2026 to stop players from gaining an unfair advantage. Players can only move their ball within a scorecard length when preferred lies are in operation. This change replaces the old rule that allowed a full club-length of relief. PGA Tour winner Michael Kim praised the decision on social media. He stated that the change "Will provide fairer outcomes during competition." The rule aims to keep the game honest for everyone.

Hadwin's mistake happened during his opening round on Thursday. He shot a one-under-par round of 70 after the penalty. Without the penalty, he would have been seven-under and just outside the top 10. He is currently tied for 24th place after a strong second round. He carded a four-under-par 67 on Friday to recover some ground. The gap to the halfway leader, Blades Brown, is now six shots.

Hadwin lost his PGA Tour card last year after making only 17 cuts in 29 starts. The 2025 FedExCup Fall standings placed him at 139th. He needs a win this week or a top-20 finish in the season-long points list. He is currently sitting 54th on the feeder circuit's standings. PGA Tour cards for the 2027 season go solely to the top 20. If he fails, he must go through PGA Tour Q-School in December.

In 2026, he has cut seven times across 13 Korn Ferry Tour starts. A runner-up finish at the Panama Championship helped his standing.

articles.title: Bears Rule Out Defensive Starter For Match-Up Vs Packers – Breaking
articles.summary: The Chicago Bears and Green Bay Packers will renew the league’s oldest rivalry on Sunday when the two teams face off inside Lambeau Field. Both of these team...
articles.body:
The Chicago Bears and Green Bay Packers will renew the league's oldest rivalry on Sunday when the two teams face off inside Lambeau Field. Both of these teams have aspirations of not only winning the NFC North, but making a deep post-season run.

That being said, it would appear Chicago will be waiting another week to get one of their long time starters back on defense. Here are the details.

The Chicago Bears will be without cornerback Kyler Gordon for Sunday's match-up against the Packers. The news comes despite the defensive back practicing in full throughout the week.

Gordon had been working his way back from a calf injury that kept him sidelined to begin the season. His return to practice offered hope that he could make his 2026 debut at Lambeau Field, but the Bears have decided he isn't ready to return to game action just yet. According to ESPN's Courtney Cronin, Gordon will remain on the physically unable to perform list rather than being activated for Sunday's NFC North showdown.

The setback is another frustrating development for Gordon, who missed significant time last season because of injuries. Chicago has been cautious with his recovery, and the team now has until October 21 to activate him from the PUP list before his return window closes. His next opportunity to play will come against the Atlanta Falcons in Week 6.

Gordon's absence means Chicago will continue without one of their key defensive backs as they prepare to face Green Bay . Chicago activated linebacker Noah Sewell from the PUP list on Saturday instead, leaving Gordon to continue working toward his return.

The two rivals are scheduled to kick off Sunday at 12 p.m. CT at Lambeau Field.

articles.title: Packers place running back Chris Brooks on injured reserve due to ankle problem
articles.summary: (AP) — Green Bay running back Chris Brooks was placed on injured reserve Saturday due to an ankle issue, an assignment that means he must miss at least the P...
articles.body:
GREEN BAY, Wis. (AP) — Green Bay running back Chris Brooks was placed on injured reserve Saturday due to an ankle issue, an assignment that means he must miss at least the Packers' next four games.

Brooks had started the Packers' 17-14 victory at Tampa Bay on Sunday and rushed for 30 yards on four carries before his injury knocked him out of the game in the second quarter.

Brooks has rushed for 70 yards on 15 attempts this season.

Earlier in the week, the Packers signed running back Pierre Strong Jr. to their active roster from their practice squad.

Strong has rushed for 499 yards and two touchdowns on 99 carries during a career that has included stints with the New England Patriots (2022) and Cleveland Browns (2023-24). Strong spent most of last season on Green Bay's practice squad.

The Packers (2-2) host the Chicago Bears (3-1) on Sunday.

articles.title: Stephen Curry drops ‘not an idiot’ take on Warriors’ roster moves
articles.summary: The Golden State Warriors are just over a week away from kicking off their 2026-27 regular season. The Warriors are entering this season without many high ex...
articles.body:
The Golden State Warriors are just over a week away from kicking off their 2026-27 regular season. The Warriors are entering this season without many high expectations after Draymond Green showed up to training camp overweight and Kristaps Porzingis continues to deal with a strange illness.

At the center of it all is Stephen Curry , who recently reiterated his commitment to the franchise with a new contract extension, and has now given his take on the team's moves, or lack thereof, over the last few years.

"I mean, I'm not an idiot. I know what it means in the sense of that window we had where coming off of '22, there were opportunities to get better, add new talent, and some worked out, some didn't. And the jury is still out on how we end this entire journey with a competitive mindset," Curry said to NBC Sports Bay Area, via Valentina Martinez of the California Post.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

The Warriors only made one major move since their 2022 championship, trading for Jimmy Butler, who is currently rehabbing a torn ACL.

Other than that, Golden State hasn't gone big game hunting often in order to give Curry a legitimate co-star in the twilight years of his career.

"I've had a really amazing career and journey. I want to win. All the other chatter doesn't necessarily matter to me in terms of how I grade our seasons," said Curry.

Curry will be hoping for better luck on the injury front this year, as he missed over 40 games last season due to a lingering knee issue.

Golden State is slated to kick off its season on October 21 with a road game vs the Los Angeles Lakers.
